lessons.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming
lessons.summary: API style shapes client flexibility, performance, team velocity, and operational complexity. REST dominates public HTTP APIs; GraphQL optimizes client-driven data fetching; gRPC excels at internal service-to-service RPC; streaming protocols handle real-time and high-throughput data flows.

sections.title: REST: Resource-Oriented HTTP
paragraphs: REST (Representational State Transfer) models APIs as resources identified by URLs, manipulated with HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), and described by standard status codes and headers. It leverages HTTP caching, CDN compatibility, and universal tooling.

REST shines for public APIs, CRUD operations, and teams wanting simplicity and broad client support. Hypermedia (HATEOAS) is rarely implemented in practice; most REST APIs are pragmatic resource endpoints with JSON bodies.

Challenges include over-fetching (returning entire objects when clients need one field), under-fetching (requiring multiple round trips), and inconsistent conventions across teams without strict API governance.

sections.title: GraphQL: Client-Specified Queries
paragraphs: GraphQL provides a single endpoint where clients send queries specifying exactly the fields they need. The server resolves a graph of types — reducing over-fetching and enabling rapid frontend iteration without backend changes for every UI tweak.

GraphQL supports mutations (writes), subscriptions (real-time via WebSocket), and introspection for schema discovery. Tools like Apollo and Relay manage caching, batching, and optimistic updates on the client.

Risks include N+1 query problems (mitigated by DataLoader batching), complex server-side resolvers, query depth/complexity attacks, and caching difficulty at the HTTP layer — POST requests bypass CDN caches by default.

sections.title: gRPC: High-Performance RPC
paragraphs: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers for compact binary serialization and HTTP/2 for multiplexed, bidirectional streaming. Service contracts are defined in .proto files, generating typed client and server stubs in multiple languages.

gRPC supports unary (request-response), server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming. It is ideal for internal microservice communication where performance, type safety, and streaming matter more than browser compatibility.

gRPC requires gRPC-Web or a proxy (Envoy) for browser clients. Debugging is harder than JSON REST — tools like grpcurl and reflection help. Load balancing uses client-side or proxy-based approaches (xDS, lookaside LB).

sections.title: Streaming: WebSockets, SSE, and Webhooks
paragraphs: Server-Sent Events (SSE) push server-to-client updates over a persistent HTTP connection — simpler than WebSockets, unidirectional, auto-reconnect built in. Ideal for live feeds, progress updates, and notifications.
WebSockets provide full-duplex communication — chat, collaborative editing, gaming. Scaling WebSockets requires sticky connections or a pub/sub backplane to broadcast across server instances.

Webhooks are server-to-server HTTP callbacks — event producers POST to consumer URLs when something happens. Simple to integrate but require retry logic, signature verification, and idempotent handlers on the receiving side.

sections.title: Choosing and Versioning APIs
paragraphs: Public mobile and web clients: REST or GraphQL depending on client diversity and data-fetching complexity. Internal service mesh: gRPC for performance. Real-time features: WebSockets or SSE. Third-party integrations: REST webhooks.

Many organizations use REST/GraphQL at the edge and gRPC internally — an API gateway translates between them. Version APIs explicitly: URL path (/v2/users), header (Accept-Version), or schema evolution with backward compatibility.
Document APIs with OpenAPI (REST), GraphQL schema SDL, or proto files. Contract testing (Pact, Buf) catches breaking changes before deployment.

expert.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming — Expert Notes
paragraphs: Expert considerations for REST, GraphQL, gRPC & Streaming: multi-region behavior, cost envelopes, and edge cases under overload.

concepts: REST: resources, HTTP verbs, status codes, cacheable GET
GraphQL: schema, queries, mutations, subscriptions, resolver graph
gRPC: Protocol Buffers, HTTP/2, four streaming modes
SSE: unidirectional server push over HTTP
WebSockets: bidirectional persistent connection
Webhooks: server-to-server event callbacks
API versioning: URL, header, schema evolution
Over-fetching vs under-fetching trade-offs
DataLoader pattern for GraphQL N+1 prevention
gRPC-Web for browser compatibility
practices: Use REST for public CRUD APIs with good HTTP semantics and caching
Use GraphQL when many client types need different field subsets
Use gRPC for internal services with high throughput requirements
Define API contracts in OpenAPI, GraphQL SDL, or proto files — generate code
Implement rate limiting and query complexity limits on GraphQL endpoints
Verify webhook signatures (HMAC) and make handlers idempotent
Version APIs before external consumers depend on them
pitfalls: GraphQL exposing entire database schema without authorization per field
gRPC without deadlines/timeouts — cascading hangs across services
REST APIs that ignore HTTP caching semantics (no ETag, no Cache-Control)
WebSockets without a scale-out strategy — connections stuck on one node
Breaking API changes without versioning or deprecation period
Using POST for all GraphQL queries without complexity analysis — DoS vector

examples.title: Netflix-style API layering
examples.description: Mobile and web clients hit a GraphQL BFF (Backend for Frontend) that aggregates data from internal gRPC microservices. The BFF handles auth, field resolution, and caching. Internal services communicate via gRPC with mTLS — never exposed publicly.

examples.title: Stripe-style webhooks
examples.description: Stripe POSTs signed webhook events to merchant endpoints on payment success. Merchants verify HMAC signatures, return 200 quickly, and process asynchronously via a queue. Idempotency keys prevent duplicate order fulfillment on webhook retry.

keyTakeaways: REST is the default for public HTTP APIs — simple, cacheable, universal
GraphQL gives clients query flexibility at the cost of server complexity
gRPC is the internal workhorse for typed, high-performance RPC
Streaming protocols (SSE, WebSockets) serve real-time use cases
Version and document APIs from day one — contract tests prevent breakage
Hybrid architectures (GraphQL edge + gRPC internal) are common at scale
lessons.whyItMatters: API choices affect latency budgets, developer experience, security surface, and deployment coupling. Wrong choices create frontend bottlenecks (REST over-fetching), operational nightmares (unbounded GraphQL queries), or integration friction (gRPC exposed to browsers). Interviewers expect nuanced comparisons, not 'always use REST.'
reflectionQuestions: When does GraphQL's flexibility become a performance or security problem?
Why do large companies use gRPC internally but REST or GraphQL externally?
How would you scale WebSocket connections across a cluster of servers?
What versioning strategy would you use for a public API with mobile clients?

lessons.title: Clean Architecture & DDD
lessons.summary: Clean Architecture and Domain-Driven Design (DDD) organize code around business domains rather than technical frameworks. This lesson covers hexagonal architecture, dependency inversion, bounded contexts, aggregates, and the tactical patterns that keep core business logic testable, framework-independent, and aligned with how the business actually works.

sections.title: Clean Architecture: Dependencies Point Inward
paragraphs: Robert Martin's Clean Architecture organizes code into concentric rings. The innermost ring is the domain — entities and business rules that would exist even if you had no database, no web framework, and no UI. Each outer ring depends on the inner rings, never the reverse. Frameworks, databases, and UI are details that belong on the outside.

The Dependency Inversion Principle makes this work: high-level modules (business logic) define interfaces (ports); low-level modules (database adapters, HTTP handlers) implement them. Your OrderService depends on an IOrderRepository interface defined in the domain layer; PostgreSQLOrderRepository in the infrastructure layer implements it.

The payoff is testability and longevity. You can unit-test business rules without spinning up a database. You can swap PostgreSQL for MongoDB by writing a new adapter. When your web framework releases a breaking version, the domain layer doesn't change.
bullets: Entities: core business objects with identity and lifecycle (Order, Customer, Account)
Use cases / application services: orchestrate domain logic for a specific user action
Interface adapters: controllers, presenters, gateways that translate between layers
Frameworks & drivers: web framework, ORM, message broker — outermost, most replaceable

sections.title: Hexagonal Architecture: Ports and Adapters
paragraphs: Alistair Cockburn's Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters) expresses the same idea with a vivid metaphor: the application core is a hexagon with ports (interfaces) on each side. Adapters plug into those ports — a REST controller adapter on one side, a PostgreSQL repository adapter on another, a Kafka event publisher on a third.

Primary (driving) adapters initiate interaction: HTTP controllers, CLI commands, message consumers. Secondary (driven) adapters respond to the core's needs: database repositories, email senders, external API clients. The core knows nothing about HTTP status codes or SQL syntax.

This symmetry makes the architecture explicit in your folder structure: domain/ contains entities and ports; application/ contains use cases; adapters/inbound/ and adapters/outbound/ contain framework-specific code. New team members can navigate by business concept, not by technology.
bullets: Port: an interface the core defines (OrderRepository, PaymentGateway, EventPublisher)
Adapter: a concrete implementation for a specific technology (PostgresOrderRepository, StripePaymentGateway)
Primary adapter: drives the application (HTTP handler calls CreateOrderUseCase)
Secondary adapter: driven by the application (use case calls repository.save())

sections.title: Domain-Driven Design: Strategic Patterns
paragraphs: Eric Evans' Domain-Driven Design distinguishes strategic design (how large systems are divided) from tactical design (how code is structured within a boundary). The strategic cornerstone is the bounded context: a explicit boundary within which a particular domain model is defined and consistent.

In an e-commerce platform, 'Product' means different things in different contexts: the Catalog context cares about descriptions and images; the Inventory context cares about stock counts and warehouse locations; the Pricing context cares about cost, margin, and discounts. Forcing one Product model across all three creates confusion and coupling.

Context maps document relationships between bounded contexts: Shared Kernel (shared code), Customer-Supplier (upstream/downstream), Conformist (downstream adopts upstream model), Anti-Corruption Layer (translates foreign models). These relationships guide integration decisions when building microservices or modular monoliths.
bullets: Ubiquitous language: developers and business stakeholders use the same terms in code and conversation
Bounded context: scope where a domain model is internally consistent
Context map: visual diagram of how bounded contexts relate and integrate
Anti-corruption layer: translation layer preventing foreign domain models from leaking in

sections.title: Domain-Driven Design: Tactical Patterns
paragraphs: Within a bounded context, tactical patterns structure the domain model. Entities have identity that persists over time (Order #12345). Value objects are defined by their attributes, not identity — Money($10, USD), Address, DateRange. They are immutable and interchangeable.

Aggregates are clusters of entities and value objects treated as a single consistency boundary. An Order aggregate contains OrderLineItems; you never modify a line item directly — you load the Order, call order.addItem(), and save the whole aggregate. This ensures invariants (total price matches sum of items) are always enforced.

Domain events capture something meaningful that happened in the domain: OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, InventoryReserved. They enable loose coupling between aggregates and bounded contexts. Domain services handle operations that don't naturally belong to a single entity (e.g., transferring funds between two Accounts).
bullets: Entity: object with unique identity (Customer, Order, Shipment)
Value object: immutable, defined by attributes (Email, Money, GeoCoordinate)
Aggregate root: the single entry point for modifying an aggregate (Order is root; LineItem is not accessed directly)
Repository: persistence abstraction that retrieves and saves aggregates as whole units
Domain event: record of a significant state change within the domain

sections.title: Applying Clean Architecture and DDD in Practice
paragraphs: These patterns are not all-or-nothing. A CRUD admin panel doesn't need aggregates and domain events. A payment processing core benefits enormously from them. Apply DDD tactically where business complexity is highest — the domain experts care deeply about correctness there.

Common project structure: src/domain/ (entities, value objects, repository interfaces, domain events), src/application/ (use cases, DTOs, application services), src/infrastructure/ (database adapters, message broker adapters, external API clients), src/interfaces/ (HTTP controllers, GraphQL resolvers, CLI).

Testing strategy follows naturally: unit tests for domain logic (fast, no I/O), integration tests for adapters (real database in test container), end-to-end tests for critical user flows. Most tests should live at the unit level because the domain layer contains the business rules that matter most.

concepts: Clean Architecture: concentric layers with dependencies pointing inward toward the domain
Dependency Inversion: high-level modules define interfaces; low-level modules implement them
Hexagonal Architecture: application core connected via ports and adapters
Bounded context: explicit boundary where a domain model is consistent
Ubiquitous language: shared vocabulary between developers and domain experts
Entity vs. value object: identity-based vs. attribute-based domain objects
Aggregate: consistency boundary grouping entities and value objects under a root
Domain event: immutable record of a significant business occurrence
Anti-corruption layer: translation boundary protecting your domain from external models
Repository pattern: abstract persistence behind a domain-centric interface
practices: Define ubiquitous language terms in a glossary shared with product and business teams
Place business rules in the domain layer — never in controllers or database triggers
Design aggregates small enough to load and save in one transaction
Use value objects for concepts like Money, Email, and Address to enforce invariants at construction
Define repository interfaces in the domain layer; implement them in infrastructure
Publish domain events from aggregate roots when state changes meaningfully
Apply DDD tactically to complex core domains; use simpler patterns for CRUD periphery
pitfalls: Anemic domain model: entities are data bags with all logic in service classes — defeats the purpose of DDD
Over-sized aggregates: loading an entire Customer with all Orders, Payments, and Addresses kills performance
Bounded context bleed: one team's model silently used by another without translation
Framework-driven design: letting ORM annotations and controller decorators define your architecture
Premature DDD: applying aggregates and context maps to a simple CRUD app adds complexity without benefit
Ignoring the context map: integrating bounded contexts without explicit relationship strategy

examples.title: Amazon's Bounded Contexts
examples.description: Amazon's platform spans dozens of bounded contexts — Catalog, Ordering, Fulfillment, Payments, Recommendations — each with its own model of core concepts. 'Product' in Catalog (marketing copy, images) differs from 'Product' in Fulfillment (weight, dimensions, hazmat flags). Anti-corruption layers translate between them at integration points.

examples.title: Clean Architecture in a Payment Service
examples.description: A payment service's domain layer defines Payment (entity), Money (value object), and PaymentGateway (port). The application layer has ProcessPaymentUseCase. Infrastructure provides StripeGateway and PostgresPaymentRepository. The domain can be fully tested with mock adapters — no Stripe API or database required.

keyTakeaways: Organize code around business domains, not technical layers or frameworks
Dependencies must point inward — the domain never imports infrastructure
Bounded contexts prevent a single overloaded model from serving every use case
Aggregates enforce consistency boundaries — always modify through the root
Ports and adapters make the core testable and technology-swappable
Apply DDD where business complexity is high; keep CRUD areas simple
Ubiquitous language bridges the gap between code and business stakeholders
lessons.whyItMatters: Systems outlive frameworks. The average web framework has a 5–10 year dominance cycle; business rules persist for decades. Clean Architecture and DDD protect your most valuable asset — business logic — from being entangled with replaceable infrastructure. In system design interviews and real projects, demonstrating domain-centric thinking signals senior-level engineering judgment.
reflectionQuestions: Identify two bounded contexts in a system you know. How does the same concept (e.g., 'User' or 'Product') differ between them?
Where in your current codebase does business logic leak into controllers or ORM models? How would you move it inward?
Design an aggregate for a library book lending system. What is the root? What invariants must it enforce?
When would an anti-corruption layer be necessary vs. simply calling another service's API directly?

lessons.title: Monolith to Microservices
lessons.summary: Most successful systems start as a monolith and evolve toward microservices only when organizational scale, deployment independence, or technical constraints demand it. This lesson teaches you how to recognize the right moment to split, how to decompose safely, and which complementary patterns — modular monoliths, event-driven architecture, CQRS, and event sourcing — fit each stage of growth.

sections.title: The Monolith Spectrum: From Big Ball of Mud to Modular Monolith
paragraphs: A monolith is not a single architecture — it is a deployment model. At one end sits the 'big ball of mud': tangled code with no clear boundaries, where every change risks breaking unrelated features. At the other end is the modular monolith: one deployable unit with well-defined internal modules, explicit interfaces between them, and enforced dependency rules.

The modular monolith gives you most of the development speed of a single codebase — shared types, atomic refactors, simple debugging — while preserving logical boundaries that can later become service boundaries. Teams that skip this step and jump straight to microservices often recreate the monolith's coupling across network calls, but now with latency, partial failures, and distributed transactions added on top.

Before considering microservices, ask: can we enforce module boundaries in code? Can we deploy independently within the monolith using feature flags? Can we scale the entire application horizontally behind a load balancer? If yes, you may not need to split yet.
bullets: Single deployable artifact: one build pipeline, one runtime, one database (often)
In-process calls: nanosecond latency, ACID transactions across modules
Modular monolith: package-by-feature, dependency rules (e.g., domain cannot import infrastructure)
Anti-pattern: 'distributed monolith' — many services that must deploy together

sections.title: When and How to Extract Microservices
paragraphs: Microservices earn their complexity when a bounded part of your system has genuinely different scaling, deployment, or team ownership needs. Classic signals include: one module needs 10× the CPU of everything else; one team wants daily deploys while another needs monthly stability; a component uses a different runtime (Python ML pipeline vs. Java API); or regulatory isolation requires separate audit boundaries.

The Strangler Fig pattern is the safest extraction path: build a new service alongside the monolith, route a slice of traffic to it via a proxy or feature flag, migrate data incrementally, and retire the old code path only when the new service is proven. Never attempt a 'big bang' rewrite — history shows these fail more often than they succeed.

Each extracted service should own its data. Shared databases between services recreate coupling and make independent deployment impossible. Start with read-heavy, loosely coupled domains (notifications, search indexing, reporting) before tackling core transactional paths like payments or inventory.
bullets: Identify bounded contexts (from DDD) as candidate service boundaries
Extract along seams that already have async communication (events, queues)
Use an API gateway or BFF (Backend for Frontend) to aggregate client-facing calls
Plan for synchronous vs. asynchronous inter-service communication upfront

sections.title: Event-Driven Architecture and Loose Coupling
paragraphs: In a microservices landscape, direct HTTP calls between dozens of services create brittle dependency graphs — a failure in the recommendation service should not block checkout. Event-driven architecture decouples producers from consumers: the Order Service publishes an OrderPlaced event; Inventory, Email, Analytics, and Fraud services react independently.

Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SNS/SQS) provide durability, replay, and fan-out. Design events as past-tense facts ('OrderPlaced', 'PaymentCaptured') rather than commands ('ProcessOrder'), so multiple consumers can react without the producer knowing who listens.

The trade-off is eventual consistency. When a user completes checkout, their order confirmation email may arrive seconds later. Your UX and business logic must tolerate this — show optimistic UI, use idempotent consumers, and design compensating transactions for failures.
bullets: Choreography: services react to events without a central orchestrator
Orchestration: a saga coordinator sequences steps (use for complex multi-step flows)
Outbox pattern: write events to a DB table in the same transaction as business data, then publish asynchronously
Dead letter queues capture poison messages for investigation

sections.title: CQRS and Event Sourcing: When Reads and Writes Diverge
paragraphs: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) separates the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries). In a simple CRUD app, one model suffices. But when read patterns differ radically from write patterns — a write-heavy order system with complex analytics dashboards — separate models let you optimize each independently.

Event sourcing takes this further: instead of storing current state, you store an append-only log of state-changing events. Current state is derived by replaying events. This gives you a complete audit trail, temporal queries ('what did the account look like on March 1?'), and natural integration with event-driven systems.

These patterns add significant complexity. Use CQRS when read/write load profiles genuinely differ or when you need multiple read-optimized projections. Use event sourcing when auditability, replay, or temporal queries are core requirements — not because it sounds architecturally impressive.
bullets: Write model: normalized, enforces invariants, handles business rules
Read model: denormalized projections optimized for specific queries (materialized views)
Projections rebuild from the event log when schemas change
Snapshots prevent replaying millions of events on every read

sections.title: Serverless and the Continuum of Decomposition
paragraphs: Serverless (FaaS) is the extreme end of decomposition: individual functions triggered by events, scaled to zero, billed per invocation. It fits spiky, stateless workloads — image processing, webhook handlers, scheduled jobs — but struggles with long-running processes, persistent connections, and cold-start-sensitive latency requirements.

Architecture is a continuum, not a binary choice. A typical mature system might run a modular monolith for core business logic, microservices for independently scaling components, serverless for event reactions, and a shared event bus tying them together. The goal is the minimum decomposition that solves your actual constraints.

Measure before splitting. If your monolith handles 500 req/s with p99 latency under 100ms and deploys weekly without conflict, microservices will slow you down. If three teams block each other on every release and one module consumes 80% of infrastructure budget, targeted extraction will pay for itself within quarters.

expert.title: Monolith to Microservices — Expert Notes
paragraphs: Expert considerations for Monolith to Microservices: multi-region behavior, cost envelopes, and edge cases under overload.

concepts: Monolith: single deployable unit — simplest ops, hardest to scale teams independently
Modular monolith: enforced internal boundaries without network overhead
Microservices: independently deployable, scalable, and failure-isolated services
Bounded context: a DDD boundary where a domain model is consistent and autonomous
Strangler Fig pattern: incrementally replace monolith functionality with new services
Event-driven architecture: services communicate via asynchronous domain events
Saga pattern: coordinate distributed transactions via compensating actions
CQRS: separate read and write models optimized for different access patterns
Event sourcing: store state changes as an immutable append-only event log
Serverless (FaaS): event-triggered functions with automatic scaling and pay-per-use billing
practices: Start with a modular monolith; enforce package boundaries and dependency rules from day one
Extract services along existing bounded contexts, not along technical layers (don't split 'the database service')
Each microservice owns its data store — no shared databases between services
Publish domain events as past-tense facts; keep event schemas backward-compatible
Use the Strangler Fig pattern for migration — never big-bang rewrite
Design for failure: timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breakers on every synchronous call
Measure team velocity, deployment frequency, and infrastructure cost before and after splitting
pitfalls: Premature microservices: splitting before team size or scaling needs justify the operational overhead
Distributed monolith: services so coupled they must deploy together, but now with network latency
Shared database anti-pattern: multiple services writing to the same tables breaks independent deployment
Chatty services: chains of synchronous HTTP calls that multiply latency and failure rates
Ignoring eventual consistency: assuming distributed systems behave like a single ACID database
Over-engineering with event sourcing when simple CRUD and audit logs would suffice

examples.title: Shopify's Modular Monolith
examples.description: Shopify runs one of the largest Ruby on Rails monoliths in production, serving millions of merchants. They invest heavily in modular boundaries (component-based architecture) and horizontal scaling rather than premature service extraction. Their lesson: monoliths scale further than most teams assume when modularized well.

examples.title: Netflix's Microservices Evolution
examples.description: Netflix migrated from a monolithic DVD rental app to 700+ microservices on AWS. Each service owns its data, communicates via REST and async events, and deploys independently — thousands of times per day. They extracted services when scaling, fault isolation, and team autonomy demands exceeded what the monolith could support.

examples.title: Uber's Domain-Oriented Microservices
examples.description: Uber decomposed around business domains (Rider, Driver, Eats, Freight) rather than technical layers. Each domain team owns services end-to-end. Cross-domain communication uses gRPC for synchronous calls and Kafka for async events, with explicit schema registries to prevent breaking changes.

keyTakeaways: Monoliths are a valid and often optimal choice for early-stage and mid-size systems
Modular monoliths preserve simplicity while preparing clean extraction boundaries
Split services when scaling, deployment, or team autonomy needs exceed monolith capacity
Event-driven architecture decouples services but introduces eventual consistency
CQRS and event sourcing are powerful but should be applied to specific problems, not by default
The Strangler Fig pattern is the safest path from monolith to microservices
Architecture is a continuum — mix monolith, microservices, and serverless where each fits best
lessons.whyItMatters: Architecture style is one of the highest-impact and hardest-to-reverse decisions in system design. Premature microservices drain velocity with operational complexity; a neglected monolith becomes unmaintainable. Understanding the full spectrum — and the signals for when to move — lets you choose consciously and evolve gracefully as your system and organization grow.
reflectionQuestions: What signals in your current (or a hypothetical) project would indicate it's time to extract a microservice?
Draw the dependency graph of services in a system you know. Where are the synchronous chains that would cause cascading failures?
For an e-commerce checkout flow, which steps could be eventual (async) and which must be synchronous? Why?
When would you choose event sourcing over a traditional database with an audit log table?

lessons.title: Caching Strategies & Layers
lessons.summary: Caching trades freshness for speed at every layer of the stack — browser, CDN, reverse proxy, application, and database. The right strategy depends on read/write ratios, consistency tolerance, and failure modes. Poor cache design causes stale data bugs, thundering herds, and memory exhaustion.

sections.title: Why and Where to Cache
paragraphs: Caching stores copies of expensive-to-compute or expensive-to-fetch data closer to the consumer. A database query taking 50 ms might be served from Redis in 1 ms or from a browser cache in 0 ms. At scale, caching is not optional — it is how systems survive.

Caches exist at multiple layers. Browser caches use HTTP headers (Cache-Control, ETag). CDNs cache static assets and cacheable API responses at edge PoPs globally. Reverse proxies (Nginx, Varnish) cache upstream responses. Application caches (Redis, Memcached) hold hot keys in memory. Database buffer pools cache pages internally.

Each layer has different TTL semantics, invalidation mechanisms, and consistency guarantees. A coherent caching strategy defines what is cached where, how long it lives, and how it is invalidated when source data changes.

sections.title: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Back
paragraphs: Cache-aside (lazy loading): the application checks the cache first. On miss, it loads from the database, populates the cache, and returns. On write, the application updates the database and deletes or updates the cache entry. This is the most common pattern — simple and flexible.

Write-through: every write goes to cache and database synchronously. Reads always hit warm cache. Consistency is strong between cache and DB, but writes are slower. Used when read-heavy workloads demand guaranteed cache freshness.

Write-back (write-behind): writes go to cache first; cache asynchronously flushes to the database. Maximizes write throughput but risks data loss if the cache fails before flush. Suitable for write-heavy, eventually-durable workloads like buffering analytics events.
bullets: Cache-aside: app manages cache; best general-purpose pattern
Write-through: synchronous DB + cache write; strong consistency
Write-back: async flush; high write throughput, durability risk

sections.title: Invalidation and the Thundering Herd
paragraphs: Cache invalidation is notoriously difficult. Time-based expiry (TTL) is simple but serves stale data until expiry. Event-driven invalidation (pub/sub, message queues) is precise but requires wiring every write path to emit invalidation events.

The thundering herd (cache stampede) occurs when a popular key expires and thousands of concurrent requests miss the cache simultaneously, each hitting the database. Mitigations include probabilistic early expiration, request coalescing (single-flight pattern), and mutex locks per key.

Versioned cache keys (e.g., product:123:v5) allow atomic invalidation by bumping a version counter instead of deleting keys. Negative caching stores 'not found' results to protect against repeated lookups for missing entities.

sections.title: Distributed Caching with Redis
paragraphs: Redis and Memcached provide shared, in-memory caches accessible to all application instances. Redis adds persistence options, rich data structures, pub/sub, and Lua scripting for atomic operations.

Size caches appropriately: too small causes constant eviction and low hit rates; too large wastes memory and money. Monitor hit rate, eviction rate, memory usage, and latency p99. Target 90%+ hit rates for well-chosen keys.

Redis Cluster and client-side consistent hashing distribute keys across shards. Hot keys — a single key receiving disproportionate traffic — require replication, local caching, or key splitting strategies.

concepts: Cache hit vs miss and hit rate as primary metric
Cache-aside, write-through, write-back patterns
TTL-based vs event-driven invalidation
Thundering herd and single-flight deduplication
CDN edge caching and Cache-Control headers
ETag and conditional requests for bandwidth savings
Negative caching for absent keys
Redis data structures: strings, hashes, sorted sets
Hot key problem in distributed caches
Cache penetration, breakdown, and avalanche scenarios
practices: Set TTLs on every cache entry — unbounded caches grow until they crash
Use single-flight or locking to prevent thundering herds on hot keys
Cache at the highest layer possible (CDN before Redis before DB)
Monitor hit rate, eviction rate, and memory; alert on sudden drops
Invalidate or version keys on write — do not rely on TTL alone for critical data
Size Redis with headroom for peak traffic and avoid maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru without understanding evictions
Test cache failure modes: what happens when Redis is entirely unavailable?
pitfalls: Caching without TTL and running out of memory
Invalidating cache after DB write fails — serving stale data indefinitely
Caching large objects that evict the entire working set
Ignoring cache consistency during database failover
Using the same TTL for rapidly changing and static data
Caching personalized data at CDN layer without Vary headers

examples.title: Product catalog with CDN + Redis
examples.description: Product images and static JSON are CDN-cached with 24-hour TTL. Product details are cache-aside in Redis with 5-minute TTL and event invalidation on price updates. Search results are not cached — they change too frequently and are user-specific.

examples.title: Leaderboard with write-back
examples.description: Game scores write to Redis sorted sets immediately for real-time leaderboard display. A background job flushes aggregated scores to PostgreSQL every 30 seconds. Acceptable data loss window: 30 seconds of scores if Redis fails — mitigated by Redis persistence (AOF).

examples.title: Preventing thundering herd on flash sale
examples.description: A popular product key uses single-flight: on cache miss, one request fetches from DB while others wait on the same promise. Combined with probabilistic early refresh (refresh at 90% of TTL), the DB never sees a spike of 10,000 concurrent queries.

keyTakeaways: Cache at every layer — browser, CDN, app, database buffer pool
Cache-aside is the default; write-through when read consistency is critical
Invalidation is harder than population — design it with every write path
Guard against thundering herds with single-flight and early expiration
Monitor hit rates and plan for cache cluster failures
Not everything should be cached — skip highly volatile or personalized data
lessons.whyItMatters: A well-designed cache reduces database load by 10–100× and cuts user-facing latency dramatically. A poorly designed cache causes subtle stale-data bugs that are hard to reproduce and catastrophic overload events when caches fail open. Caching appears in virtually every system design interview and every production performance investigation.
reflectionQuestions: What happens during a cache stampede when a popular key expires?
When is write-through preferable to cache-aside?
How would you cache user-specific data without serving one user's data to another?
What is your fallback when the entire Redis cluster is down?

lessons.title: Indexes, Replication & Sharding
lessons.summary: Indexes accelerate queries at the cost of write overhead and storage. Replication provides availability, fault tolerance, and read scaling. Sharding partitions data across nodes for write scaling — but introduces cross-shard query complexity and hot spot risk. These three mechanisms are the primary toolkit for scaling databases.

sections.title: Indexes: How Queries Find Data Fast
paragraphs: Without an index, finding a row by email requires a full table scan — O(n) pages read. A B+ tree index on email reduces this to O(log n) — typically 3–4 page reads for billions of rows. Indexes are separate data structures (usually B+ trees) storing indexed columns plus a pointer to the row (primary key or physical location).

Composite indexes (a, b, c) support queries filtering on prefix columns — useful for WHERE a = ? AND b = ? but not WHERE b = ? alone (left-prefix rule). Column order matters: put equality filters first, range filters last.

Covering index: the index contains all columns needed by the query — the engine satisfies the query from the index alone (index-only scan), avoiding heap/table lookups. CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (col) in PostgreSQL adds non-key columns to leaf pages.

Index trade-offs: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update affected indexes — more indexes = slower writes and more storage. Partial indexes (WHERE active = true) and expression indexes (LOWER(email)) target specific query patterns efficiently.
bullets: Primary key index: unique, often clustered (InnoDB) or separate (PostgreSQL)
Secondary index: non-unique, points to PK or row location
Hash index: O(1) equality only, no range scans (PostgreSQL hash, Redis)
GIN/GiST: specialized indexes for full-text, JSON, geospatial (PostgreSQL)

sections.title: Query Planning and Index Selection
paragraphs: The query optimizer (planner) estimates cost of execution plans — seq scan vs index scan vs bitmap scan — using statistics (row counts, value distribution, index correlation). Outdated statistics cause bad plans; ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) or AUTO ANALYZE keeps them fresh.

Index scan: walk B+ tree to find matching keys, fetch rows. Bitmap index scan: collect TID bitmap from index, sort by physical location, fetch in batch — reduces random I/O for moderate selectivity. Seq scan: read all pages — often faster for large fraction of table (optimizer threshold ~5–30% depending on config).

EXPLAIN ANALYZE is your diagnostic tool — shows actual vs estimated rows, index usage, and sort methods. 'Seq Scan on users' on a 10M row table for a high-selectivity query means missing or unused index.

Anti-patterns: indexing every column, redundant indexes (a,b) when (a,b,c) suffices for prefix queries, functions on indexed columns without expression index (WHERE LOWER(email) = ? bypasses index on email).

sections.title: Replication: Availability and Read Scaling
paragraphs: Replication copies data from a leader (primary) to followers (replicas). Purposes: failover when leader dies, read scaling by routing SELECTs to replicas, geographic distribution for low-latency reads.

Synchronous replication: leader waits for follower acknowledgment before commit — no data loss on failover but higher write latency and availability risk if follower is slow. Asynchronous: leader commits immediately, replicates in background — lower latency but possible data loss if leader fails before replication (RPO > 0).

Leader-follower (primary-replica) is most common: PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL binlog replication, Redis replication. Multi-leader: writes to any node, conflict resolution needed — rare, used in multi-datacenter (CouchDB, some CRDT systems). Leaderless (Dynamo-style): write to W of N nodes, read from R of N; R + W > N gives read-your-writes consistency.

Replication lag: async replicas fall behind under write load. Reading stale data from replica causes 'post redirect GET shows old profile' bugs. Monitor lag (seconds behind primary); route consistency-sensitive reads to primary or use quorum reads.
bullets: Failover: promote replica to leader — manual or automatic (Patroni, Orchestrator)
Split-brain: two nodes think they are leader — use fencing, quorum, or STONITH
Read replica: scale reads, not writes — all writes still go to leader
Chain replication: A → B → C reduces leader fan-out

sections.title: Sharding: Horizontal Partitioning for Write Scale
paragraphs: When a single node cannot handle write throughput or storage, partition data across shards — each shard is an independent database holding a subset of keys. Application or proxy layer routes queries by shard key.

Shard key choice is the most critical decision. Good key: high cardinality, even distribution, aligns with query patterns (most queries filter by shard key). Bad key: low cardinality (country=US for 95% of users), monotonically increasing (timestamp — all writes hit last shard), or unrelated to access pattern (causes cross-shard joins).

Cross-shard queries are expensive: aggregating across all shards, JOINs between sharded tables, global secondary indexes (maintained asynchronously). Design schemas so co-located data shares a shard key — user_id shards user profile, orders, and settings together.

Resharding: when adding nodes, remapping keys requires moving data. Consistent hashing minimizes remapping — only K/n keys move when adding K nodes to n existing. Virtual nodes improve balance. Tools: Vitess, Citus, MongoDB sharding, application-level routing.

sections.title: Putting It Together in Production
paragraphs: Typical evolution: single PostgreSQL with indexes → add read replicas for analytics and read-heavy endpoints → cache hot data in Redis → shard when write/storage limits hit. Each step adds operational complexity — do not shard prematurely.

Hot spots: even with good shard key, celebrity users or viral content concentrate load on one shard. Mitigations: sub-sharding hot keys, read replicas for hot shard, application-level fan-out, or splitting hot entity across synthetic keys.

Global systems combine replication (availability, geo-reads) and sharding (write scale). CockroachDB and Spanner shard automatically with distributed consensus. Application-level sharding (Vitess, custom) offers control at the cost of routing logic.

For interviews: articulate index strategy for access patterns, replication mode for RPO/RTO requirements, and shard key with awareness of hot spots and cross-shard query cost. Draw the data flow: write → leader → async replica → cache invalidation.

core.title: Indexes: How Queries Find Data Fast
paragraphs: Without an index, finding a row by email requires a full table scan — O(n) pages read. A B+ tree index on email reduces this to O(log n) — typically 3–4 page reads for billions of rows. Indexes are separate data structures (usually B+ trees) storing indexed columns plus a pointer to the row (primary key or physical location).

Composite indexes (a, b, c) support queries filtering on prefix columns — useful for WHERE a = ? AND b = ? but not WHERE b = ? alone (left-prefix rule). Column order matters: put equality filters first, range filters last.

Covering index: the index contains all columns needed by the query — the engine satisfies the query from the index alone (index-only scan), avoiding heap/table lookups. CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (col) in PostgreSQL adds non-key columns to leaf pages.

Index trade-offs: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update affected indexes — more indexes = slower writes and more storage. Partial indexes (WHERE active = true) and expression indexes (LOWER(email)) target specific query patterns efficiently.
bullets: Primary key index: unique, often clustered (InnoDB) or separate (PostgreSQL)
Secondary index: non-unique, points to PK or row location
Hash index: O(1) equality only, no range scans (PostgreSQL hash, Redis)
GIN/GiST: specialized indexes for full-text, JSON, geospatial (PostgreSQL)

core.title: Query Planning and Index Selection
paragraphs: The query optimizer (planner) estimates cost of execution plans — seq scan vs index scan vs bitmap scan — using statistics (row counts, value distribution, index correlation). Outdated statistics cause bad plans; ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) or AUTO ANALYZE keeps them fresh.

Index scan: walk B+ tree to find matching keys, fetch rows. Bitmap index scan: collect TID bitmap from index, sort by physical location, fetch in batch — reduces random I/O for moderate selectivity. Seq scan: read all pages — often faster for large fraction of table (optimizer threshold ~5–30% depending on config).

EXPLAIN ANALYZE is your diagnostic tool — shows actual vs estimated rows, index usage, and sort methods. 'Seq Scan on users' on a 10M row table for a high-selectivity query means missing or unused index.

Anti-patterns: indexing every column, redundant indexes (a,b) when (a,b,c) suffices for prefix queries, functions on indexed columns without expression index (WHERE LOWER(email) = ? bypasses index on email).

core.title: Replication: Availability and Read Scaling
paragraphs: Replication copies data from a leader (primary) to followers (replicas). Purposes: failover when leader dies, read scaling by routing SELECTs to replicas, geographic distribution for low-latency reads.

Synchronous replication: leader waits for follower acknowledgment before commit — no data loss on failover but higher write latency and availability risk if follower is slow. Asynchronous: leader commits immediately, replicates in background — lower latency but possible data loss if leader fails before replication (RPO > 0).

Leader-follower (primary-replica) is most common: PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL binlog replication, Redis replication. Multi-leader: writes to any node, conflict resolution needed — rare, used in multi-datacenter (CouchDB, some CRDT systems). Leaderless (Dynamo-style): write to W of N nodes, read from R of N; R + W > N gives read-your-writes consistency.

Replication lag: async replicas fall behind under write load. Reading stale data from replica causes 'post redirect GET shows old profile' bugs. Monitor lag (seconds behind primary); route consistency-sensitive reads to primary or use quorum reads.
bullets: Failover: promote replica to leader — manual or automatic (Patroni, Orchestrator)
Split-brain: two nodes think they are leader — use fencing, quorum, or STONITH
Read replica: scale reads, not writes — all writes still go to leader
Chain replication: A → B → C reduces leader fan-out

core.title: Sharding: Horizontal Partitioning for Write Scale
paragraphs: When a single node cannot handle write throughput or storage, partition data across shards — each shard is an independent database holding a subset of keys. Application or proxy layer routes queries by shard key.

Shard key choice is the most critical decision. Good key: high cardinality, even distribution, aligns with query patterns (most queries filter by shard key). Bad key: low cardinality (country=US for 95% of users), monotonically increasing (timestamp — all writes hit last shard), or unrelated to access pattern (causes cross-shard joins).

Cross-shard queries are expensive: aggregating across all shards, JOINs between sharded tables, global secondary indexes (maintained asynchronously). Design schemas so co-located data shares a shard key — user_id shards user profile, orders, and settings together.

Resharding: when adding nodes, remapping keys requires moving data. Consistent hashing minimizes remapping — only K/n keys move when adding K nodes to n existing. Virtual nodes improve balance. Tools: Vitess, Citus, MongoDB sharding, application-level routing.

examples.title: Twitter/X user timeline shard key
examples.description: User-centric data (profile, tweets by user, followers) shards by user_id — most reads are 'get user' or 'get user's tweets.' Global trending is harder — separate service aggregates, or fan-out on write to follower timelines (write amplification vs read optimization). Celebrity tweets create hot spots — dedicated caching and async fan-out pipelines handle disproportionate follower counts.

examples.title: PostgreSQL read replica for reporting
examples.description: Production app writes to primary. Nightly analytics and admin dashboards query read replica. Async lag of 1–5 seconds is acceptable for reports but not for 'did my payment go through' — those reads hit primary. Connection pooler (PgBouncer) routes by query type or separate connection strings per role.

examples.title: Vitess sharding at YouTube scale
examples.description: Vitess sits in front of many MySQL shards, providing SQL routing, resharding, and connection pooling. Shard key (e.g., user_id) embedded in schema. VSchema defines routing rules. Cross-shard queries supported but discouraged for hot paths. Demonstrates managed sharding layer vs application DIY routing.

Sharding enables write scale but shard key choice is hard to change later
Co-locate related data on the same shard to avoid cross-shard joins
Consistent hashing eases resharding; hot spots need application-level mitigation
Evolve gradually: indexes → replicas → cache → shard when metrics demand it
RPO/RTO requirements determine sync vs async replication — not one-size-fits-all

lessons.title: B+ Trees & LSM Trees
lessons.summary: Storage engines define how databases organize data on disk and in memory. B+ trees optimize for read-heavy, in-place update workloads (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB). LSM trees optimize for write-heavy, append-only workloads (RocksDB, Cassandra, LevelDB). Choosing the wrong engine shape for your access pattern is one of the costliest architectural mistakes.

sections.title: Why Storage Engine Design Matters
paragraphs: A database is not a monolith — at its core sits a storage engine responsible for persisting rows or key-value pairs, maintaining indexes, and recovering after crashes. The engine's on-disk layout determines read latency, write throughput, compression efficiency, and how the system behaves under compaction or vacuum.

Two families dominate modern systems: update-in-place B+ trees and append-only LSM (Log-Structured Merge) trees. Neither is universally superior. PostgreSQL's B+ tree excels at complex queries with range scans and secondary indexes. Cassandra's LSM tree excels at high-volume sequential writes and horizontal scaling — but range queries and updates are expensive.

Every storage engine also implements a WAL (Write-Ahead Log): before applying changes to data structures, append an durable log record. On crash, replay the WAL to recover. The WAL is sequential write — fast on both HDD and SSD — and is the foundation of durability (the D in ACID).

When designing a system, your read/write ratio, update frequency, range query needs, and tolerance for write amplification during compaction should drive engine selection — not brand familiarity or what your team used last project.

sections.title: B+ Trees: Read-Optimized, Update-in-Place
paragraphs: A B+ tree is a balanced tree where data lives only in leaf nodes; internal nodes store keys for navigation. Leaves are linked for efficient range scans. Each node typically matches a disk page (4–16 KB), so a tree of height 3–4 can index billions of keys with only 3–4 disk reads.

To insert or update, the engine finds the leaf, modifies it in place (or splits the page if full), and propagates splits upward. Reads follow the root-to-leaf path — predictable latency, excellent for point lookups and ORDER BY on indexed columns. Secondary indexes in PostgreSQL and MySQL are separate B+ trees pointing to primary key tuples.

Random writes to B+ tree pages cause write amplification at the filesystem level — updating one row may dirty an entire page. SSDs handle this better than HDDs, but sustained random write loads still wear flash and trigger garbage collection in the FTL. Buffer pools cache hot pages in RAM, minimizing disk reads.

PostgreSQL stores rows in heap files (unordered) with B+ tree indexes on top. MySQL InnoDB clusters the primary key — data rows live in the PK B+ tree leaf pages, making PK lookups very fast but secondary index lookups require two tree traversals (secondary index → PK → row).
bullets: Page-oriented: one node = one disk page, fits in buffer pool
Range scan: follow leaf sibling pointers left to right
Page split: insert into full page splits node, may cascade upward
Clustered vs non-clustered index: row data in PK tree (InnoDB) vs separate heap (PostgreSQL)

sections.title: LSM Trees: Write-Optimized, Append-Only
paragraphs: LSM trees invert the B+ tree trade-off. Writes go to an in-memory sorted structure (memtable, often a skip list or red-black tree) and an append-only WAL on disk. When the memtable fills, it is flushed as an immutable sorted SSTable (Sorted String Table) file on disk.

Reads check memtable, then search SSTables newest-to-oldest, often using Bloom filters to skip SSTables that definitely do not contain the key. Without compaction, read amplification grows linearly with the number of SSTables — unacceptable for production.

Compaction merges SSTables in the background — rewriting data to reduce duplicates (updates and deletes become tombstones), remove expired tombstones, and organize data into fewer, larger files. Compaction strategies (leveled, tiered, size-tiered) trade write amplification, read amplification, and space amplification differently.

Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB, and ScyllaDB use LSM variants. They shine when writes are inserts or append-only events, when you partition data so each node handles a subset of keys, and when you can tolerate eventual visibility of data during compactions.
bullets: Memtable: in-memory write buffer, sorted by key
SSTable: immutable on-disk sorted file, never modified in place
Bloom filter: probabilistic 'key definitely not here' to skip SSTables
Tombstone: deletion marker removed only after compaction

sections.title: Amplification and Compaction Trade-offs
paragraphs: Write amplification: bytes written to disk per byte of application data. LSM compaction rewrites the same key multiple times as it moves through levels — 10–30× write amplification is common in leveled compaction. SSD endurance and cloud IOPS billing make this a real cost.

Read amplification: disk reads per logical read. B+ tree is typically 1–3 page reads. LSM may check memtable + multiple SSTable levels + Bloom filter false positives. Read-heavy workloads on LSM without sufficient RAM for block cache suffer.
Space amplification: disk usage vs logical data size. Tombstones, duplicate versions during compaction, and snapshot isolation retain old versions until compaction cleans them.

Leveled compaction (LevelDB, RocksDB default): SSTables in level L are ~10× larger than L-1; each key appears in at most one SSTable per level — bounded read amplification, higher write amplification. Size-tiered compaction (Cassandra STCS): merge similar-sized SSTables — lower write amp, higher read amp and space amp. Incremental strategies (DTCS, ICS) target time-series data.

sections.title: Choosing and Operating Storage Engines
paragraphs: Choose B+ tree engines when: complex queries with joins and range scans dominate, updates modify existing rows frequently, strong single-node consistency is required, and working set fits mostly in buffer pool. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server fit this profile.

Choose LSM engines when: write throughput is the bottleneck, data is naturally partitioned by key, access is mostly primary-key get/put, or you need embedded storage (RocksDB inside Kafka Streams, Cockroach's Pebble). Cassandra, DynamoDB (conceptually), TiKV/RocksDB fit here.

Hybrid systems exist: MyRocks (MySQL on RocksDB) for write-heavy MySQL workloads. CockroachDB and TiDB use LSM (Pebble/RocksDB) with distributed SQL layers. ClickHouse uses merge-tree structures optimized for analytics — yet another design point.

Operational implications: B+ trees need VACUUM (PostgreSQL) or purge (InnoDB) to reclaim space from dead tuples. LSM trees need compaction tuning — stalled compaction causes read degradation and disk fill. Monitor compaction pending bytes, SSTable count, and write stall events in RocksDB.

examples.title: PostgreSQL heap + B+ tree index
examples.description: An UPDATE in PostgreSQL creates a new row version (MVCC) in the heap and updates index entries pointing to the new tuple. Old versions remain until VACUUM reclaims them. Heavy UPDATE workloads cause bloat — autovacuum must keep pace. Index-only scans avoid heap fetches when visibility map confirms all tuples on a page are visible — a B+ tree optimization for read-heavy analytics.

examples.title: Cassandra write path
examples.description: A write goes to commit log (WAL) + memtable. When memtable exceeds memtable_flush_after, it flushes to SSTable on disk. Reads merge memtable + SSTables. With size-tiered compaction, many SSTables accumulate; read latency grows until compaction merges them. Production clusters tune compaction strategy, gc_grace_seconds, and concurrent_compactors based on write rate and read SLA.

examples.title: RocksDB in Kafka Streams state store

lessons.title: Transactions & Isolation Levels
lessons.summary: Transactions group operations into atomic units that succeed or fail together. Isolation levels control what concurrent transactions can observe — trading consistency guarantees for performance. Understanding ACID, anomalies, MVCC, and locking strategies is essential for payment systems, inventory, and any shared mutable state.

sections.title: ACID: The Contract Transactions Provide
paragraphs: Atomicity: all operations in a transaction commit or none do. If transferring money debits account A but crashes before crediting B, the database rolls back the debit. Implemented via WAL and undo logs — on failure, replay undo records to restore prior state.

Consistency: transactions take the database from one valid state to another — constraints, foreign keys, and triggers hold. Note: 'C' is partly application responsibility; the DB enforces declared constraints, not all business rules.

Isolation: concurrent transactions behave as if they ran serially (in some level of approximation). The real world runs transactions in parallel for performance — isolation levels define acceptable anomalies.

Durability: once committed, data survives crashes. WAL fsync before commit acknowledgment ensures log records reach stable storage. Replication adds another durability dimension — a commit on the leader may not yet be on followers.
bullets: BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK: transaction boundaries
Single-statement auto-commit: each statement is its own transaction by default
Distributed transactions (2PC): atomicity across nodes — costly, avoided in modern microservices
Saga pattern: application-level compensation instead of 2PC across services

sections.title: Isolation Levels and Anomalies
paragraphs: SQL standard defines four isolation levels, from weakest to strongest: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable. Each prevents some anomalies but not others, with increasing locking or versioning overhead.
Dirty read: transaction T2 reads data written by T1 that T1 has not committed. If T1 rolls back, T2 acted on garbage. Prevented by Read Committed and above.
Non-repeatable read: T1 reads a row, T2 updates and commits it, T1 reads again and gets a different value. Prevented by Repeatable Read and above.

Phantom read: T1 runs a range query, T2 inserts a new row matching the range and commits, T1 re-runs the query and sees new rows. Prevented by Serializable (or snapshot isolation with careful handling in PostgreSQL).

Lost update: two transactions read-modify-write the same row; one overwrites the other without seeing its change. Not fully solved by isolation level alone — needs optimistic locking (version column) or SELECT FOR UPDATE.

sections.title: MVCC: Multi-Version Concurrency Control
paragraphs: MVCC avoids read-write blocking by keeping multiple versions of rows. Readers see a snapshot as of transaction start; writers create new versions without overwriting visible data. PostgreSQL and Oracle use MVCC; readers never block writers and writers rarely block readers.

PostgreSQL implements this with xmin/xmax system columns and tuple visibility rules. UPDATE creates a new row version; old version remains until VACUUM. Repeatable Read uses a snapshot taken at first statement (or transaction start in PostgreSQL) — same row read twice returns the same version.

MySQL InnoDB MVCC uses undo logs to reconstruct older row versions for Read View. Repeatable Read is the default — phantoms possible on index ranges without gap locks. Gap locks and next-key locks prevent phantoms but increase deadlock risk.

Snapshot isolation (SI) is often stronger than Read Committed but weaker than full Serializable — it prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads but historically allowed write skew (two transactions read disjoint sets, make consistent-looking updates that violate an invariant together). PostgreSQL 9.1+ Serializable uses SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation) to detect dangerous structures.
bullets: Read snapshot: transaction sees consistent view frozen at start
Write creates new version; old version visible to older snapshots
VACUUM / purge: reclaim versions no longer visible to any transaction
Write skew: concurrent transactions pass row checks but violate global invariant

sections.title: Pessimistic vs Optimistic Locking
paragraphs: Pessimistic locking: lock rows before modifying (SELECT FOR UPDATE, SELECT FOR SHARE). Other transactions block until lock released. Prevents lost updates and ensures exclusive access — but reduces concurrency and risks deadlocks.

Optimistic locking: read without lock, check version at commit (UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?). If version changed, retry. Good for low-contention workloads — no blocking, but retries under high contention.

Application-level locks: Redis SETNX, ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes, or advisory locks (PostgreSQL pg_advisory_lock) coordinate across services when transaction boundaries span systems. These are not ACID with the database — design idempotency and timeout carefully.

In microservices, each service owns its database — cross-service 'transactions' use sagas (choreography or orchestration) with compensating actions (cancel reservation, refund payment) rather than distributed 2PC, which blocks on failure and does not scale.

sections.title: Transactions in System Design
paragraphs: Payment and ledger systems demand Serializable or careful serial execution per account — double-spend and negative balance are unacceptable. Inventory systems need to prevent overselling — pessimistic lock on stock row or atomic decrement with CHECK (quantity >= 0).

Read-heavy dashboards can use Read Committed or even read replicas with lag acceptance — stale analytics is tolerable. Session state and shopping carts tolerate eventual consistency; checkout does not.

Long-running transactions are dangerous: they hold locks or old snapshots, block VACUUM (PostgreSQL xact wraparound risk), and increase deadlock probability. Keep transactions short — do validation and external API calls outside the transaction when possible.

When interviewing, state your isolation choice explicitly: 'Bank transfer: Serializable or SELECT FOR UPDATE on both accounts in consistent order to prevent deadlock.' 'Social feed like count: eventual consistency, no transaction needed.' This demonstrates intentional trade-offs.

paragraphs: Expert considerations for Transactions & Isolation Levels: multi-region behavior, cost envelopes, and edge cases under overload.

concepts: ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted → Committed → Repeatable Read → Serializable
Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update
MVCC: multi-version concurrency, snapshot reads without blocking writes
SELECT FOR UPDATE: pessimistic row lock
Optimistic locking: version column check at update time
WAL and undo log: atomicity and crash recovery mechanisms
Write skew: anomaly under snapshot isolation
Saga: distributed transaction alternative with compensating actions
2PC: two-phase commit for cross-node atomicity — high latency, blocking
practices: Use the weakest isolation level that meets correctness requirements — do not default to Serializable everywhere
Keep transactions short — no external HTTP calls or user think-time inside BEGIN...COMMIT
Prevent lost updates with version columns or SELECT FOR UPDATE on contested rows
Acquire locks in consistent order (account ID ascending) to prevent deadlocks
Use idempotency keys for retried operations in payment and order flows
Monitor long-running transactions and lock wait times in production
Prefer sagas over 2PC for cross-service workflows; design compensating actions
pitfalls: Assuming READ COMMITTED prevents lost updates — it does not without explicit locking
Long transactions blocking VACUUM in PostgreSQL — leads to table bloat and txid wraparound
Serializable isolation without handling serialization failures — apps must retry on 40001
Distributed transactions (2PC) across microservices — blocks, fragile, avoid in favor of sagas
Optimistic locking under high contention — retry storms degrade performance
Reading from async replica for financial balance checks — replication lag causes wrong decisions

examples.title: Bank transfer with row locks
examples.description: Transfer $100 from A to B: BEGIN; SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (A,B) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE; validate A >= 100; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = A; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = B; COMMIT. Lock ordering by ID prevents deadlock when two transfers cross (A→B and B→A simultaneously). Serializable isolation would also work but may retry on conflict.

examples.title: Inventory oversell with Read Committed
examples.description: Two checkout requests read stock=1 concurrently under Read Committed. Both pass validation. Both decrement. stock=-1. Fix: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock >= 1 RETURNING stock — atomic check-and-decrement, or SELECT FOR UPDATE before decrement. Isolation level alone is insufficient; the write must be conditional.

examples.title: E-commerce order saga
examples.description: Place order spans Order Service, Payment Service, Inventory Service. Instead of 2PC: Order creates pending order → Payment charges card → Inventory reserves stock → Order confirms. On payment failure: compensating cancel order. On inventory failure: refund payment, cancel order. Each step is local ACID; global consistency is eventual with defined failure paths.

keyTakeaways: ACID defines transaction guarantees — durability and atomicity rely on WAL
Weaker isolation = better performance but more anomalies — choose intentionally
MVCC enables concurrent reads and writes without blocking — PostgreSQL's core model
Lost updates require explicit locking or conditional writes, not just isolation level
Keep transactions short; long transactions harm VACUUM, locks, and throughput
Microservices use sagas with compensation, not distributed 2PC
Match isolation to business risk: payments strict, analytics relaxed
lessons.whyItMatters: Every system with shared mutable state — wallets, inventory, seat booking, idempotency keys — depends on transaction design. Bugs from wrong isolation level cause double charges, overselling, and data corruption that no amount of caching or load balancing fixes. Interviewers ask 'how do you prevent double-spend' and 'what isolation level' because these separate engineers who understand concurrency from those who treat the database as a black box.

What isolation level would you use for a financial ledger, and how would you handle serialization failures?
Explain write skew with a concrete example (e.g., on-call schedule, budget approval).
When is a saga with compensating transactions preferable to a single database transaction?

lessons.title: Architecture, Failures & Trade-offs
lessons.summary: Architecture is the art of choosing trade-offs under constraints. No design optimizes everything — you balance latency vs consistency, availability vs durability, simplicity vs flexibility. This lesson provides a framework for structuring designs, reasoning about failure modes, and articulating trade-offs clearly in reviews and interviews.

sections.title: A Structured Approach to System Design
paragraphs: After requirements and estimation, proceed in layers: (1) high-level components and data flow, (2) API and data model, (3) deep dives on the hardest problems, (4) bottlenecks and scale plan, (5) failure modes and monitoring. This sequence keeps interviews organized and ensures you don't optimize details before defining scope.

Start with a simple design that meets functional requirements for moderate scale — single app server, one database, cache optional. Then evolve: 'at 10× traffic, the database becomes the bottleneck → read replicas and cache; at 100×, shard by user_id.' Iterative scaling narrative shows you won't over-engineer day one but have a credible growth path.

Draw data flow for critical paths: user action → API → business logic → storage → async side effects. Mark sync vs async boundaries, cache layers, and external dependencies. One diagram for happy path; annotate failure behavior on the same diagram.

Identify the 2–3 core entities and their relationships. Resist designing every feature — depth on timeline generation beats breadth on 15 minor endpoints. Interviewers probe where you go deep, not how many boxes you draw.
bullets: Layer 1: clients, load balancer, app tier, storage, async pipeline
Layer 2: API contracts, schema, indexes for access patterns
Layer 3: deep dive — the hardest NFR (feed, search, consistency)
Evolution narrative: what breaks at 10×, 100×, 1000×

sections.title: CAP, PACELC, and Consistency Models
paragraphs: CAP theorem: in a network partition, you choose Consistency (all nodes see same data) or Availability (every request gets a response). Partition tolerance is mandatory in distributed systems — the real choice is CP (ZooKeeper, etcd, strongly consistent DB during partition) vs AP (Cassandra, Dynamo-style, available with divergent state merged later).

PACELC extends CAP: else (even without partition), you choose Latency or Consistency. Most systems are PA/EL — available during partition, low latency when network is fine, accepting eventual consistency. This matches most user-facing products where 100ms matters more than immediate global consistency.

Consistency models in practice: strong (linearizable reads/writes), causal (see your own writes and related ordering), read-your-writes (session stickiness or version check), eventual (converge after delay). Pick per operation: inventory deduction strong; view count eventual; user profile read-your-writes.

Don't cite CAP as excuse without specifics. Say: 'like counts use eventual consistency with periodic sync — stale by seconds is acceptable; payment status uses strong consistency via synchronous DB transaction.' Tie model to user-visible behavior.
bullets: CP: consistent during partition, may reject requests (etcd, Spanner)
AP: available during partition, reconcile later (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
PACELC: without partition, latency vs consistency trade-off
Per-operation consistency — not one choice for entire system

sections.title: Designing for Failure
paragraphs: Everything fails: servers, disks, networks, deployments, humans. Design assumes failure is normal. Redundancy: N+1 or N+2 for critical tiers — multiple app instances across AZs, database with automatic failover, multi-AZ object storage. Single points of failure (one Redis node, one cron leader) must be identified and eliminated or accepted with documented risk.

Timeouts everywhere: client → service, service → database, service → external API. Without timeouts, one slow dependency blocks thread pools and cascades. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter for idempotent operations — never unbounded retry storms. Circuit breakers fail fast when downstream is unhealthy.

Idempotency keys for writes: client sends Idempotency-Key header; server deduplicates within TTL window. Essential for payment APIs and any at-least-once delivery (Kafka consumers, webhook retries). Without idempotency, retries double-charge or duplicate records.

Graceful degradation: if recommendations fail, show popular items; if search is down, browse categories. Define fallback behavior per dependency. Bulkheads isolate thread pools so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all resources. Health checks and load balancer draining remove unhealthy instances before total collapse.
bullets: Failover: automatic promotion of replica (RDS, Redis Sentinel)
Blast radius: limit impact of one failure (AZ isolation, cell architecture)
Chaos engineering: inject failures to validate assumptions (Netflix Simian Army)
Runbooks: documented response for each alert — not improvised during outage

sections.title: Common Architectural Trade-offs
paragraphs: Push vs pull for fan-out: push (write-time fan-out to follower timelines) gives fast reads but expensive writes for celebrities; pull (assemble timeline at read time) saves writes but slow reads; hybrid (push for normal users, pull for celebrities) is Twitter's approach. Trade-off: read latency vs write amplification vs implementation complexity.

SQL vs NoSQL: relational for ACID, joins, complex queries; document/wide-column for horizontal scale, flexible schema, high write throughput. Polyglot persistence is normal — Postgres for transactions, Elasticsearch for search, Redis for cache, S3 for blobs.

Sync vs async: sync simplifies client mental model (request → response includes result) but couples latency and availability; async (queue, webhook, polling) decouples and absorbs spikes but complicates UX (job status, notifications). Choose async when side effects are slow, optional, or fan out to many systems.

Build vs buy: managed services (RDS, SQS, CloudFront) reduce ops burden and accelerate MVP; self-hosted (Kafka cluster, custom CDN) offers control and cost at scale. Trade-off: engineering time vs operational ownership vs vendor lock-in.
bullets: Write amplification vs read optimization — pick based on read/write ratio
Normalization vs denormalization — joins vs duplicate data for read speed
Strong consistency cost: coordination, latency, reduced availability during partition
Operational complexity: microservices vs monolith team velocity trade-off

sections.title: Presenting and Defending Your Design
paragraphs: Lead with the core flow, then justify each major component: 'Redis cache here because 95% of reads are hot keys; 90% hit rate cuts DB load 10×.' Anticipate challenges: 'What if cache fails? DB absorbs load — we have headroom to 2×; alerts fire; degrade non-critical features.'

Name trade-offs explicitly: 'We chose eventual consistency for likes because strong consistency would require distributed locking on every click, adding 50ms latency for negligible user benefit.' Unnamed trade-offs look like oversights.

Scope management: when interviewer adds 'also support real-time notifications,' acknowledge, prioritize against MoSCoW, extend diagram incrementally rather than restarting. 'I'll add a WebSocket gateway and notification service fed by the existing event bus — deferring mobile push provider integration to phase 2.'
Close with monitoring and success criteria: metrics, alerts, SLIs/SLOs. Architecture without observability is incomplete — you cannot operate what you cannot measure.

Close with monitoring and success criteria: metrics, alerts, SLIs/SLOs. Architecture without observability is incomplete — you cannot operate what you cannot measure.

Require idempotency keys on all non-read APIs that mutate state
Identify single points of failure; eliminate or document accepted risk

examples.title: Hybrid timeline fan-out (Twitter model)
examples.description: Normal users (< 10K followers): push tweets to follower timeline Redis lists on write — O(followers) write, O(1) read. Celebrities: pull at read time from celebrity's tweet list merged with pushed timelines. Trade-off: bounded write amplification while keeping read latency under 200ms for 99% of users.

examples.title: Payment service CP design
examples.description: During network partition, payment service rejects writes rather than risk double-spend or inconsistent balances. Strong consistency via Postgres serializable isolation + idempotency keys. Availability sacrificed for financial correctness — explicit CP choice with user-facing 'try again' messaging.

examples.title: Circuit breaker on third-party SMS
examples.description: SMS provider latency degrades from 200ms to 30s. Circuit breaker opens after 50% error rate in 10s window. Notification service queues messages locally, returns success to user ('notification pending'), drains queue when circuit half-open probes succeed. Graceful degradation — email fallback if SMS unavailable > 5 min.
