lessons.title: The Design → Build → Measure Loop
lessons.summary: System design does not end at deployment. The best architects treat design as a continuous loop: hypothesize, build minimally, measure against SLOs, learn, and iterate. This lesson connects design frameworks to operational reality — load testing, observability, postmortems, and evolutionary architecture that adapts as requirements and traffic change.

sections.title: From Design Doc to MVP
paragraphs: A design document captures intent: requirements, architecture diagram, data model, failure modes, and open questions. It is a proposal, not a contract. The MVP implements must-have functional requirements at modest scale with explicit non-goals — 'no multi-region, no full-text search, single AZ database with nightly backups.'

Build the simplest architecture that validates the core hypothesis: do users want this feature? Can we meet latency targets at 1K QPS? Premature optimization wastes weeks; missing critical path design (wrong data model, unshardable schema) wastes months. Focus MVP engineering on reversible decisions and hard-to-change foundations (data model, API contracts).

Feature flags decouple deployment from release — ship code dark, enable for 1% of users, measure, expand. Strangler patterns apply within monoliths: new code path behind flag, old path default, migrate traffic incrementally. Design docs should specify flag strategy and rollback plan for risky changes.
Define 'done' for MVP with measurable criteria: p99 < 300ms at 500 QPS load test, error rate < 0.1%, core user journey E2E tests pass. Without exit criteria, MVP scope creeps indefinitely.
bullets: Design doc: requirements, diagram, schema, risks, open questions
MVP: must-haves only; explicit non-goals documented
Reversible vs irreversible decisions — invest design time accordingly
Feature flags: deploy != release; enable gradual rollout

sections.title: Measuring What Matters: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
paragraphs: SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a measured metric: request latency, availability, throughput, correctness. SLO (Service Level Objective) is a target: 99.9% of requests complete in < 200ms over 30 days. SLAs are contractual SLOs with penalties — internal teams use SLOs without legal binding.

Error budget = 100% - SLO. At 99.9% availability, you have 0.1% budget (~43 minutes downtime/month). Budget exhausted → freeze features, focus on reliability. Budget healthy → take more deployment risk. This framework aligns product velocity with reliability mathematically.

Choose SLIs users feel: availability (successful responses / total), latency (p99 of server-side duration), freshness (age of data in async pipeline). Avoid vanity metrics (CPU average) as primary SLOs — correlate to user experience.

Instrument from day one: structured logs, metrics (Prometheus/Datadog), distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry). Design docs should list golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) per component before build starts — retrofitting observability is expensive.
bullets: Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation (Google SRE)
SLO: target over rolling window (30 days common)
Error budget: remaining allowable unreliability before SLO breach
RED method: Rate, Errors, Duration for request-driven services

sections.title: Load Testing and Validation
paragraphs: Load tests validate capacity assumptions before users do. Types: smoke (minimal, CI), load (expected peak), stress (beyond peak to find breaking point), soak (sustained hours — memory leaks, connection exhaustion), spike (sudden 10× burst). Match test profile to estimated traffic shape.

Test in production-like environment — staging with 10% of prod data size often lies about query plans and cache behavior. Use anonymized production data snapshots or synthetic generators that reproduce skew (hot keys, celebrity users).

Measure during tests: p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, resource saturation (CPU, memory, disk IOPS, connection pool usage, Kafka lag). Compare against design doc estimates. Gap analysis drives next iteration: 'estimated 10K QPS; stress test knee at 4K — database write lock contention.'

Chaos and fault injection in staging: kill a replica, inject latency to dependencies, partition network. Validate failover, circuit breakers, and degradation paths designed on paper actually work. A design untested under failure is hope, not engineering.
bullets: k6, Locust, Gatling — programmatic load test scripts in CI
Production traffic shadowing/mirroring — test new path with real traffic safely
Gradual rollout: canary 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% with automated rollback
Load test failure is success — you found the bottleneck before users did

sections.title: Learning from Production: Postmortems and Iteration
paragraphs: Blameless postmortems document incidents: timeline, root cause, contributing factors, action items. Focus on systems and processes, not individuals. 'Database failover took 15 minutes because runbook was stale' → action: automate failover + quarterly drill.

Postmortem action items feed the design loop: add cache layer, increase timeout, fix idempotency bug, shard hot table. Architecture evolves from production pain — the best designs are revised, not born perfect.

Continuous profiling (CPU, memory, lock contention) in production finds regressions invisible in averages. A deployment that adds 5ms p99 doesn't trip error alerts but erodes SLO over weeks. Compare canary metrics to baseline automatically during rollout.

Capacity review cadence: quarterly re-run estimation with growth metrics. Traffic 3× in six months? Revisit shard plan before emergency. Technical debt register tracks shortcuts taken in MVP with remediation triggers ('shard when write QPS > 5K').
bullets: Blameless culture: fix systems, not punish people
Five whys: dig from symptom to root cause
Action items: specific, owned, dated — tracked to completion
Game days: scheduled disaster recovery exercises

sections.title: Evolutionary Architecture and Knowing When to Redesign
paragraphs: Evolutionary architecture supports guided change: fitness functions (automated architecture tests) enforce rules ('domain layer cannot import infrastructure'). Modular monoliths evolve into services when metrics justify — not on a calendar.

Recognize redesign triggers: sustained SLO breach despite optimization, org structure outgrows architecture (Conway's Law), fundamental schema change needed, cost curve nonlinear. Incremental refactor (Strangler Fig) beats rewrite unless technical debt is existential.

Document architecture decision records (ADRs): context, decision, consequences, status. Future teams understand why Kafka was chosen over RabbitMQ in 2024 and when to revisit. Design loop includes revisiting ADRs when assumptions change.
The meta-skill: hold design lightly. Measure ruthlessly. Iterate quickly. Systems that survive are not the most elegant initial design — they are the ones whose teams learned fastest from reality.

examples.title: MVP → scale iteration for a startup API
examples.description: MVP: monolith + Postgres, SLO 99.5% / 500ms p99. Month 3: p99 degrades to 800ms at 2K QPS — load test reproduces; add Redis cache for hot reads, p99 back to 200ms. Month 9: write QPS nears 3K — add read replica, async job queue for emails. Month 18: shard users table by user_id. Each step triggered by SLO breach or capacity review, not premature planning.

examples.title: Error budget freeze before holiday season
examples.description: E-commerce platform has 99.95% availability SLO. October error budget at 15% remaining before Black Friday freeze. Team defers risky database migration to January, focuses on load test remediation and runbook drills. December traffic 5× — SLO met. Budget framework prevented a risky change during critical window.

examples.title: Postmortem-driven architecture change
examples.description: Outage: payment webhook consumer fell behind, 4-hour delay in order confirmations. Root cause: single-threaded consumer, no dead letter queue, poison message blocked partition. Actions: horizontal consumer scaling, DLQ, idempotency keys, alert on consumer lag > 1 min. Design loop turned incident into durable architecture improvement.

lessons.title: Requirements & Capacity Estimation
lessons.summary: Every system design begins before boxes and arrows: clarify requirements, define success metrics, and estimate scale. This lesson teaches a structured approach to functional vs non-functional requirements, back-of-the-envelope capacity math, and the assumptions you must state explicitly so your architecture stands up to scrutiny in interviews and design reviews.

sections.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
paragraphs: Functional requirements describe what the system does: users can post tweets, search products, transfer money. Non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe how well: latency under 200ms p99, 99.99% availability, GDPR compliance, support 10M DAU. Architecture is driven as much by NFRs as by features — a chat app and a batch analytics pipeline share 'store messages' but diverge radically on latency and consistency.

Explicitly categorize requirements into must-have (MVP), should-have (near-term), and could-have (future). In a 45-minute interview, scope to must-haves plus one differentiating NFR. Ask clarifying questions: Who are the users? Read vs write ratio? Geographic distribution? Durability expectations if a datacenter fails?

Constraints narrow the solution space: budget, team size, existing tech stack, regulatory environment, time to market. A startup with three engineers should not design Google-scale sharding on day one. Document constraints as actively as requirements — they explain why you chose a monolith over 50 microservices.

Success metrics translate NFRs into measurable targets: p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, throughput (QPS), availability (nines), data durability (RPO/RTO), cost per request. Without numbers, 'fast' and 'scalable' are meaningless and impossible to validate after build.
bullets: Functional: features and behaviors
Non-functional: latency, availability, consistency, durability, compliance
MoSCoW prioritization: Must, Should, Could, Won't (this session)
RPO/RTO: acceptable data loss and recovery time on failure

sections.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
paragraphs: Capacity estimation grounds architecture in physics and economics. Start with daily active users (DAU), actions per user per day, and peak-to-average ratio (often 2–3×, higher for events like New Year's Eve). Convert to peak QPS: if 100M DAU each post 2 times/day, writes = 200M/day ≈ 2,300 avg QPS; at 3× peak ≈ 7,000 write QPS.

Know handy constants: 1 day ≈ 86,400 seconds (~100K for quick math); 1 million seconds ≈ 11.5 days; 1 GB = 10^9 bytes (or 2^30 for memory — state which). SSD random read ~100 μs; sequential ~1 GB/s; datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms same region, ~150 ms cross-continent; memory ~100 ns access.

Storage estimation: average object size × objects retained × replication factor. 500 bytes per tweet × 500M tweets/day × 365 days × 3 replicas ≈ 274 TB/year before compression. Does it fit one Postgres instance? No — partition, archive, or object storage.

Bandwidth: average response size × QPS. 10 KB response × 100K QPS = 1 GB/s egress — significant cost and CDN requirement. Estimation reveals bottlenecks early: a 1 KB write triggering 50 KB of fan-out read is a architectural red flag at scale.
bullets: Peak QPS = (DAU × actions/day × peak factor) / 86400
Storage = object_size × volume × retention × replication
Bandwidth = response_size × read_QPS (+ upload for writes)
Memory cache: working set size — what fraction of data is hot?

sections.title: Capacity Planning for Compute, Storage, and Cache
paragraphs: Compute: a single modern server handles ~1–10K simple HTTP req/s depending on work. 100K read QPS / 5K per server ≈ 20 app servers + load balancer overhead. CPU-bound workloads (video encode, ML inference) scale differently — profile per core throughput.

Database sizing: Postgres comfortable ~5–10K simple reads/s or ~1–2K writes/s on tuned hardware before sharding. Redis ~100K ops/s per node for simple commands. Disk IOPS limits random write throughput — WAL and index updates matter. Don't assume linear scale; measure knee points.

Cache hit ratio dramatically reduces backend load. If 90% of reads hit CDN/Redis, 100K read QPS becomes 10K database QPS — the difference between one cluster and ten. Estimate working set: if 20% of users are active daily and each accesses 50 keys, that's DAU × 0.2 × 50 hot keys (with skew — 80/20 rule applies).

State assumptions explicitly: 'assuming 100M DAU, 10:1 read/write, 500 byte records, 5 year retention, 99.9% availability.' Reviewers and future you can revisit when assumptions change. Wrong assumptions are fine; unstated ones cause production surprises.

sections.title: API Design and Data Model Implications
paragraphs: Requirements drive API shape. Read-heavy feeds favor cursor pagination and precomputed timelines. Write-heavy logs favor append-only ingestion and async processing. Search requirements imply inverted indexes (Elasticsearch) beyond primary storage.

Entity relationships emerge from use cases: User posts Tweet, User follows User, Tweet has Likes. Identify access patterns before schema: 'get timeline for user' (read fan-out), 'get likes for tweet' (counter or aggregate), 'search tweets by keyword' (secondary index). Each pattern maps to storage and cache choices.

Consistency requirements per operation: liking a post can be eventually consistent (count off by one briefly); bank transfer cannot. Classify operations into strong consistency, read-your-writes, or eventual — this directly determines database choice, cache invalidation, and sync vs async boundaries.

Multi-tenancy, permissions, and audit requirements add columns, row-level security, or separate schemas. Compliance (HIPAA, PCI) may mandate encryption at rest, network isolation, and retention policies — non-negotiable constraints that affect every layer.
bullets: Access patterns first: how data is read/written drives schema and indexes
Pagination: offset (small datasets) vs cursor (infinite feeds)
Consistency tier per operation — not one global setting
Audit trail: append-only event log vs mutable rows with history tables

sections.title: Documenting and Presenting Estimates
paragraphs: In interviews, spend 5–10 minutes on requirements and estimation before drawing architecture. Verbalize math aloud; round aggressively; sanity-check orders of magnitude. Interviewers care about structured thinking, not exact digits.

A one-page capacity summary for design reviews includes: traffic (peak QPS read/write), storage (GB/TB per year), bandwidth, cache working set, and growth assumptions (2× per year?). Tie each number to a component: '7K write QPS → Kafka 20 partitions, 3 brokers; 100K read QPS → CDN + 10 Redis nodes + 5 read replicas.'

Identify the first bottleneck: usually single-database writes, hot partition, or egress cost. Propose mitigation in the design: sharding key, read replicas, CDN, async pipeline. Estimation without bottleneck analysis is arithmetic, not engineering.
Re-estimate after MVP launch with real metrics. Capacity planning is continuous — load tests validate assumptions; production traffic reveals skew and long-tail behavior estimates miss.

Know handy constants: 1 day ≈ 86,400 seconds (~100K for quick math); 1 million seconds ≈ 11.5 days; 1 GB = 10^9 bytes (or 2^30 for memory — state which). SSD random read ~100 μs; sequential ~1 GB/s; datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms same region, ~150 ms cross-continent; memory ~100 ns access.

Storage estimation: average object size × objects retained × replication factor. 500 bytes per tweet × 500M tweets/day × 365 days × 3 replicas ≈ 274 TB/year before compression. Does it fit one Postgres instance? No — partition, archive, or object storage.

Bandwidth: average response size × QPS. 10 KB response × 100K QPS = 1 GB/s egress — significant cost and CDN requirement. Estimation reveals bottlenecks early: a 1 KB write triggering 50 KB of fan-out read is a architectural red flag at scale.
bullets: Peak QPS = (DAU × actions/day × peak factor) / 86400
Storage = object_size × volume × retention × replication
Bandwidth = response_size × read_QPS (+ upload for writes)
Memory cache: working set size — what fraction of data is hot?

core.title: Capacity Planning for Compute, Storage, and Cache
paragraphs: Compute: a single modern server handles ~1–10K simple HTTP req/s depending on work. 100K read QPS / 5K per server ≈ 20 app servers + load balancer overhead. CPU-bound workloads (video encode, ML inference) scale differently — profile per core throughput.

Database sizing: Postgres comfortable ~5–10K simple reads/s or ~1–2K writes/s on tuned hardware before sharding. Redis ~100K ops/s per node for simple commands. Disk IOPS limits random write throughput — WAL and index updates matter. Don't assume linear scale; measure knee points.

Cache hit ratio dramatically reduces backend load. If 90% of reads hit CDN/Redis, 100K read QPS becomes 10K database QPS — the difference between one cluster and ten. Estimate working set: if 20% of users are active daily and each accesses 50 keys, that's DAU × 0.2 × 50 hot keys (with skew — 80/20 rule applies).

State assumptions explicitly: 'assuming 100M DAU, 10:1 read/write, 500 byte records, 5 year retention, 99.9% availability.' Reviewers and future you can revisit when assumptions change. Wrong assumptions are fine; unstated ones cause production surprises.

core.title: API Design and Data Model Implications
paragraphs: Requirements drive API shape. Read-heavy feeds favor cursor pagination and precomputed timelines. Write-heavy logs favor append-only ingestion and async processing. Search requirements imply inverted indexes (Elasticsearch) beyond primary storage.

Entity relationships emerge from use cases: User posts Tweet, User follows User, Tweet has Likes. Identify access patterns before schema: 'get timeline for user' (read fan-out), 'get likes for tweet' (counter or aggregate), 'search tweets by keyword' (secondary index). Each pattern maps to storage and cache choices.

Consistency requirements per operation: liking a post can be eventually consistent (count off by one briefly); bank transfer cannot. Classify operations into strong consistency, read-your-writes, or eventual — this directly determines database choice, cache invalidation, and sync vs async boundaries.

Multi-tenancy, permissions, and audit requirements add columns, row-level security, or separate schemas. Compliance (HIPAA, PCI) may mandate encryption at rest, network isolation, and retention policies — non-negotiable constraints that affect every layer.
bullets: Access patterns first: how data is read/written drives schema and indexes
Pagination: offset (small datasets) vs cursor (infinite feeds)
Consistency tier per operation — not one global setting
Audit trail: append-only event log vs mutable rows with history tables

core.title: Documenting and Presenting Estimates
paragraphs: In interviews, spend 5–10 minutes on requirements and estimation before drawing architecture. Verbalize math aloud; round aggressively; sanity-check orders of magnitude. Interviewers care about structured thinking, not exact digits.

A one-page capacity summary for design reviews includes: traffic (peak QPS read/write), storage (GB/TB per year), bandwidth, cache working set, and growth assumptions (2× per year?). Tie each number to a component: '7K write QPS → Kafka 20 partitions, 3 brokers; 100K read QPS → CDN + 10 Redis nodes + 5 read replicas.'

Identify the first bottleneck: usually single-database writes, hot partition, or egress cost. Propose mitigation in the design: sharding key, read replicas, CDN, async pipeline. Estimation without bottleneck analysis is arithmetic, not engineering.
Re-estimate after MVP launch with real metrics. Capacity planning is continuous — load tests validate assumptions; production traffic reveals skew and long-tail behavior estimates miss.

concepts: Functional vs non-functional requirements (NFRs)
Peak QPS: DAU × actions/day × peak factor / 86400
Read/write ratio: drives cache, replica, and CDN strategy
Working set: fraction of data actively accessed — cache sizing input
RPO/RTO: recovery point/time objectives for disaster planning
Availability nines: 99.9% = 8.7 hours downtime/year
Replication factor: storage and write amplification multiplier
Access patterns: query shapes that determine schema and indexes
Consistency tiers: strong vs eventual per operation, not globally
Back-of-envelope: orders-of-magnitude sanity check before detailed design
practices: Ask clarifying questions before designing — scope, users, read/write mix, latency targets
State all assumptions explicitly; round numbers to one significant figure
Compute peak QPS, storage/year, and bandwidth before drawing components
Classify each operation's consistency and durability requirements
Identify the first bottleneck and design mitigation for it
Use MoSCoW to prevent scope creep in time-boxed design sessions
Revisit estimates with load test results after implementation
pitfalls: Skipping requirements and jumping to microservices diagram — misses NFR-driven choices
Using average QPS instead of peak — systems fail at peak
Ignoring fan-out: one write triggering N reads multiplies load invisibly
Forgetting replication and index overhead in storage math
Treating estimation as precise — false precision hides uncertain assumptions
One global consistency model — over-provisions sync where eventual suffices

examples.title: Twitter-like timeline (interview classic)
examples.description: 300M DAU, 200M tweet/day, 5:1 read/write for timeline fetches. Write QPS ≈ 2,300 avg, 7K peak. Timeline read: 300M DAU × 20 views/day = 6B reads/day ≈ 70K avg, 200K peak. Storage: 280 bytes/tweet × 200M/day × 365 × 3 replicas ≈ 60 TB/year. Conclusion: write path is easy; fan-out read path drives cache (Redis timelines) and CDN for media.

examples.title: URL shortener capacity
examples.description: 100:1 read/write ratio, 100M new URLs/month, 10B redirects/month. Write ≈ 40/s avg; read ≈ 4,000/s avg, 12K peak. Storage: 500 bytes/URL × 1.2B URLs/year ≈ 600 GB/year — fits one DB with sharding by hash. Cache: 20% URLs get 80% traffic — Redis working set ~120M keys × 100 bytes ≈ 12 GB. Bottleneck: read QPS → Redis + CDN redirect at edge.

examples.title: Video upload platform
examples.description: 1M uploads/day, average 500 MB file. Ingress bandwidth: 1M × 500 MB / 86400 ≈ 5.8 GB/s peak ~15 GB/s. Storage: 500 TB/day raw — object storage (S3), not database. Transcoding: async worker pool; 10 min video × 5 renditions = compute-bound pipeline. Requirements drive async upload → queue → workers architecture.

keyTakeaways: Requirements and NFRs precede architecture — clarify before you draw
Back-of-envelope math reveals bottlenecks at orders-of-magnitude level
Peak QPS, not average, determines provisioning and failure behavior
Read/write ratio and fan-out dominate caching and replication strategy
State assumptions explicitly so designs can be validated and revised
Consistency and durability requirements vary per operation — classify each
Capacity planning is iterative — validate with load tests and production metrics
lessons.whyItMatters: Interviewers and principal engineers expect you to anchor architecture in numbers. Systems that skip estimation over-provision expensively or under-provision catastrophically. Structured requirements and capacity math turn vague 'build a social network' prompts into defensible designs with explicit trade-offs.
reflectionQuestions: Estimate peak QPS and storage for a note-taking app with 10M DAU, 5 notes created/user/week, 20 reads/user/day. What is the first bottleneck?
Which operations in a ride-sharing app need strong consistency vs eventual? List five and justify each.
Your estimate assumed 10:1 read/write but production shows 2:1. Which architecture components are now over- or under-provisioned?
How do RPO and RTO differ for a messaging app vs a payment ledger?

lessons.title: CAP, PACELC & Consensus
lessons.summary: Distributed systems face unavoidable trade-offs between consistency, availability, and latency. CAP and PACELC frameworks help you reason about these trade-offs consciously. Consensus algorithms like Raft keep replicas in agreement — powering everything from etcd to distributed databases.

sections.title: The Reality of Distributed Systems
paragraphs: When components run on multiple machines connected by a network, failures are normal — not exceptional. Networks partition, packets drop, nodes crash, clocks skew. A distributed system must continue operating (or fail gracefully) despite these failures.

The fundamental challenge is maintaining shared state across unreliable nodes. Should all replicas agree before responding (consistency)? Should the system keep serving requests even if some replicas are unreachable (availability)? You cannot maximize both during a network partition.

Understanding these trade-offs prevents you from choosing tools with wrong expectations — expecting strong consistency from an AP cache or five-nines availability from a CP coordination service during splits.

sections.title: CAP Theorem
paragraphs: CAP states that a distributed data store can provide at most two of three properties: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every request receives a non-error response), and Partition tolerance (the system operates despite network partitions between nodes).

In practice, partition tolerance is non-negotiable — networks fail. So the real choice during a partition is Consistency (CP) or Availability (AP). CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper, traditional RDBMS with sync replication) may reject writes or reads to preserve consistency. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB with eventual consistency) accept writes on both sides of a partition and reconcile later.
CAP is often misunderstood as a static label. Systems can be mostly AP with tunable consistency, or mostly CP with read replicas that serve stale data. Context and configuration matter.

sections.title: PACELC Extension
paragraphs: PACELC extends CAP: if there is a Partition (P), choose between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); Else (E), choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C). This captures the everyday trade-off even when the network is healthy.

Even without partitions, synchronous replication to all replicas adds latency. Many systems default to reading from the nearest replica (low latency, eventual consistency) and offer optional linearizable reads (high latency, strong consistency) per request.

DynamoDB is PA/EL by default (available during partition, low-latency eventually consistent reads). PostgreSQL with synchronous replication is PC/EC (consistent during partition, consistent but slower when healthy). Cassandra is PA/EL with tunable consistency per query.

sections.title: Consistency Models
paragraphs: Strong consistency (linearizability): every read sees the latest write — as if one copy exists. Eventual consistency: replicas converge over time; reads may return stale data temporarily. Causal consistency: preserves cause-effect ordering without full linearizability.
Read-your-writes: a user always sees their own updates. Monotonic reads: a user never sees time go backward. These session guarantees are often sufficient and cheaper than global strong consistency.
Choose consistency per operation: financial transfers need linearizability; social media like counts tolerate eventual consistency; shopping cart reads need read-your-writes.

sections.title: Consensus with Raft
paragraphs: Consensus algorithms ensure multiple nodes agree on a value or log sequence despite failures. Raft is the approachable standard: nodes are followers, one leader is elected, the leader replicates log entries to a majority quorum before committing.

Quorum (majority of nodes) ensures any two quorums overlap — at least one node has the latest committed entry. Leader election uses randomized timeouts to avoid split-brain. etcd, Consul, and CockroachDB use Raft variants.

Consensus is expensive — typically 3 or 5 nodes, limited write throughput compared to leaderless systems. Use it for coordination (service discovery, config, locks), not high-throughput data ingestion.

expert.title: CAP, PACELC & Consensus — Expert Notes
paragraphs: Expert considerations for CAP, PACELC & Consensus: multi-region behavior, cost envelopes, and edge cases under overload.

concepts: CAP: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance — pick two during partition
PACELC: Latency vs Consistency when network is healthy
CP systems: etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner (with TrueTime)
AP systems: Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), Riak
Linearizability vs eventual consistency
Read-your-writes and monotonic reads session guarantees
Raft consensus: leader election, log replication, quorum
Quorum: majority agreement for commit
Split-brain: two leaders during partition without quorum
Fencing tokens to prevent stale leaders from writing
practices: Classify each data store in your architecture as CP or AP with PACELC
Use consensus stores (etcd) only for coordination, not bulk data
Request strong consistency only on operations that require it
Run clock sync (NTP/Chrony) on all nodes — skew breaks TTL and ordering
Test partition behavior with chaos engineering (iptables, toxiproxy)
Monitor replication lag on read replicas before serving stale reads
Use fencing tokens when relying on distributed locks
pitfalls: Labeling a system 'CP' or 'AP' without understanding tunable consistency
Using etcd for high-throughput writes — it is a coordination store
Assuming read replicas return latest data without lag monitoring
Ignoring clock skew in TTL-based leases and lock expiration
Split-brain from misconfigured quorum sizes (even number of nodes)
Choosing strong consistency globally when only one operation needs it

examples.title: Kubernetes etcd
examples.description: Kubernetes stores cluster state in etcd — a CP system using Raft. During a network partition, the minority partition becomes read-only. This is acceptable because cluster coordination demands consistency over availability. Application data lives elsewhere.

examples.title: DynamoDB global tables
examples.description: Multi-region DynamoDB global tables replicate asynchronously — AP with eventual consistency across regions. A user updating profile in US-East may see stale data in EU-West for seconds. Product accepts this for profile reads; payment uses single-region strong consistency.

examples.title: Bank transfer with quorum
examples.description: A bank uses a strongly consistent store requiring quorum writes for transfers. During partition, minority nodes reject writes — users see errors rather than double-spend. Availability is sacrificed for correctness on this critical path.

keyTakeaways: Partition tolerance is mandatory — the real choice is consistency vs availability
PACELC captures latency vs consistency trade-offs during normal operation
Match consistency level to operation criticality — not everything needs linearizability
Raft and quorum-based consensus power coordination services like etcd
Test partition and failure scenarios — theoretical CAP choices meet reality in production
Read replicas and caches introduce staleness — monitor lag explicitly
lessons.whyItMatters: Every distributed database, cache, and coordination service embeds CAP/PACELC trade-offs. Misaligned expectations cause data corruption, double-spending, and split-brain incidents. System design interviews center on articulating these trade-offs for specific requirements.
reflectionQuestions: Is Redis Cluster CP or AP during a network partition?
Why does etcd use Raft for Kubernetes instead of a simple key-value store?
When is eventual consistency unacceptable for your application?
How does PACELC apply to a read from a PostgreSQL async replica?

lessons.title: Continuous Batching & Paged Attention
lessons.summary: Continuous batching keeps GPUs busy by admitting new requests as others finish tokens. Paged attention makes the KV memory layout practical at high concurrency.

sections.title: From static to continuous batching
paragraphs: Static batching waits for an entire batch to finish before admitting new work — short requests pad behind long ones. Continuous (iteration-level) batching schedules at each decode step, so finished sequences free slots immediately.

The scheduler must account for KV memory, fairness, and latency SLOs. Without memory awareness, admitting too many sequences causes OOM; without fairness, long generations starve short interactive requests.

sections.title: Paged attention
paragraphs: Paged attention stores KV in non-contiguous blocks tracked by a block table, similar to OS virtual memory. This cuts waste from reserving max-context contiguous buffers per sequence and enables sharing blocks for identical prefixes.

lessons.title: CI/CD & Observability
lessons.summary: CI/CD automates the path from code commit to production deployment. Observability — metrics, logs, and traces — tells you what your system is actually doing under load. Together they form the feedback loop that makes reliable, fast-moving engineering teams possible. This lesson covers pipeline design, deployment strategies, the three pillars of observability, and SRE-inspired alerting practices.

sections.title: Continuous Integration: Fast, Reliable Feedback
paragraphs: Continuous Integration (CI) means every code change triggers an automated pipeline that builds, tests, and validates the change before it merges. The goal is fast feedback: if a developer breaks the build, they know within minutes, not days.

A well-designed CI pipeline runs in stages ordered by cost: lint and format check (seconds) → unit tests (seconds to minutes) → integration tests with test containers (minutes) → build artifact (minutes) → security scan (minutes). Fail fast — don't run expensive integration tests if unit tests already failed.

Cache aggressively: dependency downloads (npm, Maven, Go modules), Docker layer caches, and test result caches cut pipeline time dramatically. Target under 10 minutes for CI on a typical change. Longer pipelines discourage small, frequent commits.
bullets: CI triggers: pull request opened/updated, merge to main, scheduled nightly builds
Artifact registry: store built Docker images, JARs, or binaries with immutable tags
Branch protection: require CI pass + code review before merge
Flaky test quarantine: isolate unreliable tests rather than ignoring red builds

sections.title: Continuous Delivery and Deployment Strategies
paragraphs: Continuous Delivery (CD) extends CI: every merge to main produces a deployable artifact that passes all tests. Continuous Deployment goes further — every merge auto-deploys to production. Most teams use CD with manual approval for production; true continuous deployment suits high-test-coverage, low-blast-radius systems.

Deployment strategies control risk. Rolling update replaces instances incrementally (K8s default). Blue-green deploys a parallel environment, switches traffic, and keeps the old version for instant rollback. Canary releases route a small percentage of traffic (1–5%) to the new version, monitor error rates and latency, then gradually increase.

Feature flags decouple deployment from release: deploy code to production dark (flag off), then enable for internal users, then 1% of customers, then everyone. If something breaks, flip the flag off — no redeployment needed. This is the safest way to ship risky changes.
bullets: Rolling update: incremental replacement — simple but slow rollback
Blue-green: instant traffic switch with immediate rollback capability
Canary: gradual traffic shift with automated promotion or rollback on metric thresholds
Feature flags: control feature visibility independently of deployment
Database migrations: backward-compatible changes first, then code deploy, then cleanup

sections.title: Metrics: Measuring What Matters
paragraphs: Metrics are numeric measurements over time: request rate, error rate, latency, CPU usage, queue depth. They power dashboards, alerts, and autoscaling decisions. The RED method covers request-driven services: Rate (requests/sec), Errors (failed requests/sec), Duration (latency distribution). The USE method covers resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors.

Histograms and percentiles matter more than averages. Average latency of 50ms can hide the fact that 1% of requests take 5 seconds. Track p50, p95, and p99 latency. Alert on p99, not mean — users experience tail latency, not averages.

Prometheus is the dominant open-source metrics system: pull-based scraping, PromQL query language, Grafana for visualization. OpenTelemetry provides vendor-neutral instrumentation that exports to Prometheus, Datadog, or CloudWatch. Define SLIs (Service Level Indicators) from metrics and set SLOs (Service Level Objectives) with error budgets.
bullets: RED: Rate, Errors, Duration — for request/response services
USE: Utilization, Saturation, Errors — for CPU, memory, disk, network
SLI: quantified measure of service reliability (e.g., '99.9% of requests succeed')
SLO: target for an SLI (e.g., '99.9% availability over 30 days')
Error budget: allowed unreliability before pausing feature work for reliability

sections.title: Logs and Distributed Tracing
paragraphs: Structured logging replaces free-text log lines with JSON objects containing consistent fields: timestamp, level, service, traceId, spanId, message, and contextual key-value pairs. Structured logs are searchable, filterable, and correlatable across services.

Correlation IDs (trace IDs) link logs across services. When a request enters your system, generate or propagate a trace ID. Every log line, metric, and span includes it. When debugging a failed request, search by trace ID to see the complete journey across 15 microservices.

Distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo via OpenTelemetry) records the path of a request through every service it touches. Each service creates spans (timed operations) nested under the trace. Traces reveal which service added 800ms of latency, where errors originated, and whether retries caused duplicate work.
bullets: Structured logging: JSON with consistent fields — never printf-style free text in production
Correlation/trace ID: propagated through every service call and log line
Span: a single timed operation within a trace (HTTP call, DB query, cache lookup)
OpenTelemetry: vendor-neutral SDK for metrics, logs, and traces
Log aggregation: ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), Loki, or cloud-native (CloudWatch, Datadog)

sections.title: Alerting, On-Call, and the Observability Culture
paragraphs: Alert on symptoms, not causes. 'Error rate > 1% for 5 minutes' is actionable. 'CPU > 80%' is not — high CPU might be fine during a traffic spike. Every alert should require human action; if it doesn't, it's a dashboard metric, not an alert.

Reduce alert fatigue: aggregate related alerts, use escalation policies, and review alert effectiveness monthly. If an alert fires and nobody acts on it, delete or downgrade it. On-call engineers should trust that every page is a real problem.

Observability is a culture, not a tool. Instrument code during development, not as an afterthought. Run game days (chaos engineering) to validate that your metrics, logs, and traces actually help you diagnose injected failures. Post-incident reviews (blameless postmortems) feed improvements back into monitoring and architecture.
bullets: Symptom-based alerting: error rate, latency SLO breach, availability drop
Runbooks: documented response steps linked from every alert
Blameless postmortem: focus on systemic fixes, not individual fault
Game days: inject failures (kill pods, add latency) to test observability and response
Dashboard hierarchy: service overview → service detail → infrastructure detail

Run game days (chaos engineering) to validate that your metrics, logs, and traces actually help you diagnose injected failures. Post-incident reviews (blameless postmortems) feed improvements back into monitoring and architecture.

Runbooks: documented response steps linked from every alert
Blameless postmortem: focus on systemic fixes, not individual fault
Game days: inject failures (kill pods, add latency) to test observability and response
Dashboard hierarchy: service overview → service detail → infrastructure detail

expert.title: CI/CD & Observability — Expert Notes

concepts: CI pipeline: automated build, test, and validate on every code change
CD: every merge produces a deployable artifact; deployment may be manual or automatic
Canary deployment: route small traffic percentage to new version, monitor, then promote
Feature flags: decouple code deployment from feature release visibility
RED metrics: Rate, Errors, Duration for request-driven services
USE metrics: Utilization, Saturation, Errors for infrastructure resources
SLI/SLO: Service Level Indicator (measurement) and Objective (target threshold)
Structured logging: machine-parseable JSON logs with consistent field names
Distributed tracing: end-to-end request path visibility across services via spans
OpenTelemetry: open standard for collecting metrics, logs, and traces
practices: Keep CI pipeline under 10 minutes; fail fast with cheap checks first
Use canary or blue-green deployments for production — never big-bang deploy
Deploy database migrations separately and make them backward-compatible
Instrument the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation
Use structured JSON logging with trace IDs in every service from day one
Alert on user-facing symptoms (error rate, p99 latency) not infrastructure causes (CPU)
Write a runbook for every alert; if you can't write one, the alert isn't actionable
pitfalls: No CI: manual testing and deployment leads to fear-driven release cycles
Alert fatigue: too many non-actionable alerts cause on-call engineers to ignore real pages
Logging PII or secrets: structured logs in aggregators become compliance liabilities
Average latency monitoring: hides tail latency that ruins user experience for 1% of requests
Observability as afterthought: retrofitting instrumentation after launch misses critical early data
No rollback plan: deploying without tested rollback is gambling, not engineering

examples.title: Google's SRE and Error Budgets
examples.description: Google's Site Reliability Engineering team defines SLOs with error budgets: if a service has 99.9% availability SLO, it gets 43 minutes of downtime per month. When the budget is exhausted, feature launches pause until reliability improves. This aligns product velocity with operational stability.

examples.title: Etsy's CI/CD and Feature Flags
examples.description: Etsy deploys to production dozens of times daily using continuous deployment with strong CI (thousands of tests), feature flags for gradual rollouts, and comprehensive observability. Their deployment pipeline includes automatic rollback when error rates exceed thresholds during canary phases.

examples.title: OpenTelemetry at Honeycomb
examples.description: Honeycomb pioneered observability-driven debugging using high-cardinality events (not just pre-aggregated metrics). OpenTelemetry instrumentation sends rich span data to their platform, enabling engineers to ask arbitrary questions about production behavior without pre-defining dashboards.

keyTakeaways: CI provides fast feedback; CD ensures every merge is deployable
Canary deployments and feature flags minimize the blast radius of bad releases
Metrics (RED/USE), structured logs, and traces form the three pillars of observability
Track p99 latency and error rates — averages hide the problems users actually feel
Alert on symptoms that need human action; eliminate alerts that don't
SLOs and error budgets balance feature velocity with reliability investment
Observability must be built in from the start — retrofitting is expensive and incomplete
lessons.whyItMatters: You cannot operate what you cannot see. CI/CD enables teams to ship quickly and safely; observability tells you whether what you shipped actually works. In system design, proposing a architecture without a deployment strategy or monitoring plan is incomplete — interviewers and production systems both demand this feedback loop.
reflectionQuestions: Design a CI pipeline for a microservice with unit tests, integration tests, and Docker build. What runs in which order and why?
Your canary deployment shows 0.5% error rate (baseline is 0.1%). Walk through your decision: promote, hold, or rollback?
What SLIs and SLOs would you define for a payment processing API?
A user reports a slow checkout experience. How do trace IDs and structured logs help you diagnose which service is responsible?

lessons.title: Docker, Kubernetes & Service Mesh
lessons.summary: Containers standardize how applications are packaged and run. Kubernetes orchestrates containers at scale across clusters of machines. Service meshes add a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication, security, and observability. This lesson walks through each layer — from Dockerfile best practices to Kubernetes primitives to Istio/Linkerd — and when each is worth the operational investment.

sections.title: Docker: Images, Containers, and the Build Pipeline
paragraphs: A Docker image is a layered, immutable filesystem snapshot containing your application, runtime, and dependencies. A container is a running instance of an image — isolated via Linux namespaces and cgroups, sharing the host kernel but with its own process tree, network stack, and filesystem view.

Images are built from Dockerfiles. Best practices: use multi-stage builds (compile in one stage, copy only the binary to a minimal runtime image), pin base image versions, run as a non-root user, minimize layer count, and use .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files. A Go binary in a distroless image might be 15 MB; the same app in a full Ubuntu image could be 500 MB.

Container registries (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, Harbor) store and distribute images. Tag images with git SHA or semver, not just 'latest'. Scan images for CVEs in CI before deployment. Immutable tags ensure that what you tested is exactly what runs in production.
bullets: Image layers: each Dockerfile instruction creates a cached layer — order matters for build speed
Multi-stage builds: separate build environment from runtime for smaller, more secure images
Container vs. VM: containers share the kernel (lighter, faster start); VMs have full OS isolation
docker-compose: local multi-container development; not for production orchestration

sections.title: Kubernetes Core Concepts: Pods, Deployments, and Services
paragraphs: Kubernetes (K8s) orchestrates containers across a cluster of nodes. The pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers sharing network and storage. You rarely create pods directly; instead, you declare desired state via higher-level objects and K8s reconciles reality to match.

A Deployment manages ReplicaSets that maintain a desired number of pod replicas. Rolling updates replace pods incrementally (maxUnavailable, maxSurge control the pace). Rollbacks are one command away. StatefulSets handle stateful workloads (databases) with stable network identities and persistent volumes.

Services provide stable network endpoints for pods. ClusterIP (internal only), NodePort (exposes on each node's IP), LoadBalancer (cloud provider external IP). Ingress controllers (Nginx, Traefik, AWS ALB) route HTTP traffic to services based on host and path rules, terminating TLS at the edge.
bullets: Pod: one or more containers sharing network namespace and volumes
Deployment: declarative rolling updates with desired replica count
Service: stable DNS name and load balancing across pod replicas
Ingress: HTTP/HTTPS routing rules to services with TLS termination
ConfigMap / Secret: inject configuration and sensitive data into pods
Namespace: logical cluster partition for environments or teams

sections.title: Scaling, Scheduling, and Resource Management
paragraphs: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) scales pod replicas based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics (requests per second from Prometheus). Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts resource requests/limits. Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes nodes when pods can't be scheduled.

Every pod declares resource requests (guaranteed minimum) and limits (maximum allowed). Without requests, the scheduler can't pack pods efficiently. Without limits, one runaway container can starve others on the same node. Set requests based on measured p95 usage; set limits at 2–3× requests.

Probes keep services healthy: liveness probes restart crashed containers, readiness probes remove unready pods from service load balancing, startup probes protect slow-starting apps from premature liveness kills. Always define probes — K8s defaults to 'always healthy' if you don't.
bullets: HPA: scale replicas on metrics — target 70% CPU utilization is a common starting point
Resource requests/limits: requests for scheduling, limits for enforcement (OOM kill)
Liveness probe: 'is the process alive?' — failure triggers restart
Readiness probe: 'can it handle traffic?' — failure removes from service endpoints
PodDisruptionBudget: minimum available pods during voluntary disruptions (node drain, upgrades)

sections.title: Service Mesh: Istio, Linkerd, and the Data Plane
paragraphs: As microservice count grows, cross-cutting concerns — mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, traffic splitting, distributed tracing — become painful to implement in every service. A service mesh extracts these into a dedicated infrastructure layer: a sidecar proxy (Envoy in Istio, Linkerd's micro-proxy) injected alongside each pod handles all inter-service traffic.

The control plane (Istiod, Linkerd control plane) configures proxies centrally. The data plane (sidecar proxies) executes policies without application code changes. Enable mTLS between all services with a single policy. Route 5% of traffic to a canary version via VirtualService rules. Inject trace headers automatically.

Service meshes add latency (typically 1–3ms per hop) and operational complexity. They're justified at 20+ services with strict security requirements, frequent canary deployments, or multi-cluster setups. For smaller deployments, Kubernetes Services plus a well-configured ingress may suffice.
bullets: Sidecar proxy: intercepts all inbound and outbound pod traffic
mTLS: mutual TLS authentication and encryption between every service pair
Traffic management: weighted routing, fault injection, circuit breaking via config
Observability: automatic metrics, access logs, and trace propagation
Istio: feature-rich, Envoy-based — higher resource overhead
Linkerd: lightweight Rust micro-proxy — lower latency, simpler ops

sections.title: Infrastructure as Code and GitOps
paragraphs: Manual kubectl apply doesn't scale across environments and teams. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tools — Terraform for cloud resources, Pulumi for general-purpose IaC — declare desired infrastructure in version-controlled files. Every change is reviewed, tested, and auditable.

For Kubernetes specifically, GitOps (ArgoCD, Flux) treats Git as the single source of truth. You commit K8s manifests (or Helm charts, Kustomize overlays) to a repo; the GitOps controller continuously reconciles the cluster to match. Drift is detected and auto-corrected. Rollbacks are git revert.

Helm packages K8s resources into reusable charts with templated values. Kustomize overlays let you patch base manifests for dev/staging/prod without duplication. Choose based on team preference — both are production-proven.
bullets: Terraform: declarative cloud infrastructure (VPCs, clusters, databases, IAM)
GitOps: Git repo drives cluster state — ArgoCD/Flux auto-sync on commit
Helm charts: parameterized, versioned K8s application packages
Kustomize: overlay-based manifest customization without templating

expert.title: Docker, Kubernetes & Service Mesh — Expert Notes
paragraphs: Expert considerations for Docker, Kubernetes & Service Mesh: multi-region behavior, cost envelopes, and edge cases under overload.

concepts: Docker image: layered, immutable application package built from a Dockerfile
Container: running instance of an image with isolated process, network, and filesystem
Kubernetes pod: smallest deployable unit — one or more co-located containers
Deployment: manages rolling updates and replica count for stateless applications
Service: stable network endpoint with load balancing across pod replicas
Ingress: HTTP routing and TLS termination at the cluster edge
HPA: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler — scales replicas based on resource or custom metrics
Service mesh: infrastructure layer for inter-service security, routing, and observability
Sidecar proxy: injected container that handles all pod network traffic (Envoy, Linkerd)
GitOps: continuous deployment driven by Git repository as the source of truth
practices: Use multi-stage Docker builds with minimal base images (distroless, alpine)
Pin image tags to git SHA — never deploy untagged 'latest' to production
Declare resource requests and limits on every pod; base requests on measured usage
Configure liveness, readiness, and startup probes for every service
Use namespaces to isolate environments (dev, staging, prod) or teams
Store K8s manifests in Git and deploy via GitOps for auditable, reversible changes
Adopt a service mesh when you have 20+ services or strict mTLS requirements — not before
pitfalls: Running containers as root — a container escape compromises the host node
No resource limits: one memory-leaking pod OOM-kills neighbors on the same node
Missing health probes: K8s routes traffic to pods that aren't ready to serve
Using docker-compose patterns in production instead of proper orchestration
Adopting a service mesh too early — operational overhead outweighs benefits for small deployments
Storing secrets in ConfigMaps or plain Git — use Sealed Secrets, Vault, or cloud secret managers

examples.title: Spotify's Kubernetes Migration
examples.description: Spotify migrated from bare-metal services to Kubernetes over several years, running thousands of microservices on K8s clusters. They built internal tooling (Titus) on top of K8s for developer experience, demonstrating that raw Kubernetes requires platform engineering investment to be productive at scale.

examples.title: Lyft's Envoy and Istio
examples.description: Lyft created Envoy as a high-performance sidecar proxy and contributed it to the CNCF. They use Istio service mesh for mTLS, traffic shifting during deployments, and observability across hundreds of microservices — validating the service mesh pattern at large scale.

examples.title: GitOps at Weaveworks
examples.description: Weaveworks pioneered GitOps with Flux: all cluster configuration lives in Git, changes are pull-request reviewed, and Flux automatically syncs approved commits to production. Rollbacks are instant git reverts — no manual kubectl required.

keyTakeaways: Containers package applications consistently; Kubernetes orchestrates them at scale
Declare desired state in YAML — K8s reconciles reality continuously
Deployments, Services, and Ingress are the minimum K8s primitives every engineer should know
Resource requests/limits and health probes are non-negotiable for production workloads
Service meshes solve cross-cutting inter-service concerns but add complexity — adopt when justified
GitOps and IaC make infrastructure changes auditable, repeatable, and reversible
Invest in platform engineering — raw K8s is powerful but not developer-friendly out of the box
lessons.whyItMatters: Kubernetes is the de facto standard for container orchestration in production. Whether you operate clusters directly or deploy to managed services (EKS, GKE, AKS), understanding pods, services, scaling, and deployment strategies is essential. Service mesh and GitOps knowledge distinguishes engineers who can design production-grade platforms from those who can only write application code.
reflectionQuestions: Walk through what happens when you kubectl apply a Deployment with 3 replicas — how does K8s achieve the desired state?
Your service has p99 latency spikes during deployments. How would a service mesh help with canary releases?
What would you put in a Dockerfile multi-stage build for a Node.js API vs. a Go microservice?
When would managed container services (ECS Fargate, Cloud Run) be a better choice than self-managed Kubernetes?

lessons.title: Queues, Pub/Sub & Event Streaming
lessons.summary: Messaging decouples producers from consumers in time and space, enabling async processing, resilience, and event-driven architectures. Point-to-point queues, pub/sub fan-out, and durable event logs each solve different problems — with distinct delivery guarantees that your application must handle explicitly.

sections.title: Why Messaging Matters
paragraphs: Synchronous request-response ties the caller's fate to the callee's availability and latency. If the email service is slow, the signup API waits — or times out. Messaging introduces a buffer: the producer publishes a message and continues; the consumer processes it when ready.

Messaging enables load leveling (spiky traffic absorbed by a queue), service decoupling (producers do not know consumers), geographic distribution, and reliable retry without blocking users. Event-driven architectures treat state changes as facts that multiple services react to independently.
The cost is complexity: delivery semantics, ordering guarantees, poison messages, schema evolution, and observability across async boundaries are harder than synchronous calls.

sections.title: Point-to-Point Queues
paragraphs: A message queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer (competing consumers model). RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, and Azure Service Bus implement this pattern. Ideal for task distribution: image processing, email sending, order fulfillment.

Queues provide natural load balancing — add more workers to drain faster. Messages persist until acknowledged (at-least-once) or until processed (with visibility timeouts in SQS). Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) capture messages that fail after max retries for manual inspection.
Ordering is generally per-queue, not global. FIFO queues (SQS FIFO) guarantee order within a message group at the cost of throughput. Design consumers to be idempotent because redelivery happens.

sections.title: Pub/Sub and Fan-Out
paragraphs: Publish/subscribe delivers one message to many subscribers. Google Pub/Sub, Amazon SNS, and Redis pub/sub fan out events to multiple interested services. A 'OrderPlaced' event might trigger inventory, shipping, analytics, and notification services simultaneously.

Pub/sub decouples event producers from the set of consumers — new subscribers can be added without changing the publisher. Message brokers handle subscription management and delivery retries per subscriber.
Ephemeral pub/sub (Redis) drops messages if no subscriber is listening. Durable pub/sub (Kafka, Google Pub/Sub) persists messages for later consumption — critical for reliability.

sections.title: Event Streaming with Kafka
paragraphs: Event streaming platforms (Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar, Amazon Kinesis) store messages in an append-only, partitioned log. Consumers track their offset and can replay history — enabling event sourcing, audit trails, and reprocessing after bug fixes.

Kafka partitions provide ordering within a partition and parallel consumption across partitions. Partition key choice (e.g., user_id) ensures related events stay ordered. Retention is time- or size-based, not consumption-based — multiple consumer groups read independently.

Kafka suits high-throughput event pipelines: click streams, CDC, log aggregation, and microservice choreography. Operational complexity is higher than SQS — you manage brokers, partitions, and consumer lag.

sections.title: Delivery Semantics and Idempotency
paragraphs: At-most-once: messages may be lost but never duplicated — fire and forget. At-least-once: messages are redelivered on failure — duplicates possible, consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: the holy grail — achieved in practice via idempotent consumers plus transactional outbox or Kafka transactions, not by the broker alone.

Design every consumer to handle duplicate messages: idempotency keys, upsert operations, or deduplication tables. Retry policies use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms.
Poison messages — permanently failing payloads — must route to DLQ after N attempts. Alert on DLQ depth. Never infinite retry loops that block queue processing.

examples.title: Order processing pipeline
examples.description: Checkout API writes order to PostgreSQL and an outbox row in one transaction. An outbox relay publishes OrderCreated to Kafka. Inventory, shipping, and email services consume from separate consumer groups — each processes independently with idempotent handlers keyed by order_id.

examples.title: Image thumbnail generation
examples.description: Upload triggers an SQS message with S3 object key. Auto-scaling worker fleet pulls messages, generates thumbnails, writes back to S3. Failed messages retry 3 times with backoff, then move to DLQ for manual review.

The outbox pattern bridges reliable DB writes with event publishing

lessons.title: Attention Cost & KV Cache
lessons.summary: Transformers spend memory and compute on attention. The KV cache is the dominant serving-memory cost during decode — system designers must treat it as a first-class resource.

sections.title: Why attention dominates the systems budget
paragraphs: Self-attention lets every token attend to every earlier token. Naively, that is quadratic in sequence length for compute and memory. Training can often afford full attention; autoregressive inference cannot casually ignore the growing key/value tensors.

During decode, each new token reuses prior keys and values. Systems cache them (the KV cache) so they are not recomputed. Cache size grows with batch × layers × heads × sequence × dtype — frequently the binding constraint on GPU memory before FLOPs are exhausted.
bullets: Prefill: process the prompt (compute-heavy)
Decode: emit tokens one-by-one (memory-bandwidth heavy)
KV cache: stored keys/values per layer for prior tokens

sections.title: Design implications
paragraphs: Paged attention (as in vLLM) treats KV blocks like virtual memory pages to reduce fragmentation. Prefix caching reuses KV for shared prompt prefixes across requests. Separating prefill and decode onto different pools can improve utilization when traffic mixes long prompts with long generations.

When estimating capacity, start from concurrent sequences × expected context × bytes per KV element × layers — then compare to HBM. Quantization (FP8/INT8/INT4) and speculative decoding change the cost curve but do not remove the need for this estimate.

lessons.title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 & HTTP/3
lessons.summary: HTTP is the dominant application-layer protocol for web and API communication. Each major version solved specific performance bottlenecks—from connection overhead in HTTP/1.1 to head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2 to TCP-level blocking in HTTP/3. Understanding these evolutions is critical for API design, CDN configuration, and performance tuning.

sections.title: HTTP/1.1: The Foundation
paragraphs: HTTP/1.1, standardized in 1997 and refined over decades, is a text-based request-response protocol. A client sends a request with a method (GET, POST, etc.), path, headers, and optional body. The server responds with a status code, headers, and body. Each request is independent and semantically meaningful—GET should be safe and idempotent, POST creates resources, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes.

HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections (keep-alive), allowing multiple requests over a single TCP connection. Before this, each request required a new TCP handshake. Keep-alive dramatically reduced latency, but HTTP/1.1 still processes responses in order on each connection—if one request is slow, subsequent responses queue behind it (head-of-line blocking at the application layer). Browsers worked around this by opening 6–8 parallel connections per domain, which itself caused congestion.

Headers carry critical metadata: Content-Type defines the body format, Authorization carries credentials, Cache-Control directs caching behavior, and Set-Cookie establishes session state. Status codes communicate outcomes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301 Moved Permanently, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable. Designing APIs with correct semantics—using the right status codes, methods, and cache headers—is a hallmark of production-quality engineering.
bullets: Idempotent methods: GET, PUT, DELETE — safe to retry without side effects
Conditional requests: If-None-Match (ETag) and If-Modified-Since enable efficient caching
Chunked transfer encoding: stream response bodies without knowing total size upfront

sections.title: HTTP/2: Multiplexing and Binary Framing
paragraphs: HTTP/2, published in 2015, addressed HTTP/1.1's performance limits while maintaining semantic compatibility. The key innovation is multiplexing: many request-response streams share a single TCP connection simultaneously. Streams are independent—slow Stream A doesn't block Stream B. Data is split into binary frames tagged with stream IDs, enabling efficient parsing and eliminating the need for multiple parallel connections.

HTTP/2 also introduced header compression (HPACK), server push (server proactively sends resources), and stream prioritization. In practice, server push saw limited adoption (browsers deprecated it) because preload hints and HTTP caching proved more effective. Header compression, however, is significant—API requests with large JWT tokens or cookie headers benefit substantially.

The critical limitation HTTP/2 didn't solve: TCP-level head-of-line blocking. TCP guarantees ordered byte delivery. If one packet is lost, all subsequent packets on that connection stall until retransmission completes—even if they belong to different HTTP/2 streams. On lossy networks (mobile, cross-continent), this can negate HTTP/2's multiplexing benefits. This limitation directly motivated HTTP/3.
bullets: ALPN negotiation: TLS handshake advertises h2 (HTTP/2) or http/1.1 support
Single TCP connection per origin reduces handshake overhead and memory
Flow control at both connection and stream levels prevents receiver overwhelm

sections.title: HTTP/3: QUIC over UDP
paragraphs: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a transport protocol built on UDP. QUIC implements its own reliability, congestion control, and encryption (TLS 1.3 is integrated into the handshake, reducing setup to ~1 RTT or 0-RTT for resumed connections). Most importantly, QUIC multiplexes streams independently—packet loss on one stream doesn't block others, solving TCP's head-of-line blocking problem.

QUIC also enables connection migration: if a client's IP changes (switching from Wi-Fi to cellular), the connection persists via a connection ID rather than breaking on the 4-tuple change. For mobile users, this is transformative. Connection establishment is faster too—QUIC combines transport and TLS handshakes, and 0-RTT resumption allows sending data in the first packet for returning clients.

Adoption is accelerating: Cloudflare, Google, and major CDNs support HTTP/3. However, some corporate firewalls and middleboxes block or throttle UDP, causing fallback to HTTP/2. sections.title: Caching, CDNs, and Performance
paragraphs: HTTP caching is one of the most impactful performance optimizations available. Cache-Control headers (max-age, s-maxage, no-cache, no-store, private, public) control how long responses are cached at browsers, CDNs, and reverse proxies. ETags enable conditional requests—clients send If-None-Match and receive 304 Not Modified instead of the full body. For read-heavy APIs serving relatively static data, aggressive caching can reduce origin load by 90%+.

Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) cache content at edge locations geographically close to users. A user in Tokyo hits a Tokyo edge server instead of your US-based origin. paragraphs: RESTful API design maps domain concepts to HTTP resources and methods. Collections use plural nouns (/users, /orders), individual resources use IDs (/users/123). Response bodies should be consistent—wrap collections in a standard envelope if your team agrees on a convention.

Versioning strategies include URL path (/v1/users), headers (Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=1), or query parameters. URL versioning is simplest and most visible. Rate limiting via 429 status with Retry-After headers protects your service. CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin) are required for browser-based clients calling APIs on different domains—a common source of frontend integration bugs.

In microservices, HTTP is often the default inter-service protocol for its simplicity, debuggability (curl, browser dev tools), and universal support. However, for high-throughput internal communication, gRPC (covered in a later lesson) may be preferable. The choice depends on team familiarity, performance requirements, and whether you need browser compatibility.

core.title: HTTP/1.1: The Foundation
paragraphs: HTTP/1.1, standardized in 1997 and refined over decades, is a text-based request-response protocol. A client sends a request with a method (GET, POST, etc.), path, headers, and optional body. The server responds with a status code, headers, and body. Each request is independent and semantically meaningful—GET should be safe and idempotent, POST creates resources, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes.

HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections (keep-alive), allowing multiple requests over a single TCP connection. Before this, each request required a new TCP handshake. Keep-alive dramatically reduced latency, but HTTP/1.1 still processes responses in order on each connection—if one request is slow, subsequent responses queue behind it (head-of-line blocking at the application layer). Browsers worked around this by opening 6–8 parallel connections per domain, which itself caused congestion.

Headers carry critical metadata: Content-Type defines the body format, Authorization carries credentials, Cache-Control directs caching behavior, and Set-Cookie establishes session state. Status codes communicate outcomes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 301 Moved Permanently, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable. Designing APIs with correct semantics—using the right status codes, methods, and cache headers—is a hallmark of production-quality engineering.

Conditional requests: If-None-Match (ETag) and If-Modified-Since enable efficient caching
Chunked transfer encoding: stream response bodies without knowing total size upfront

core.title: HTTP/2: Multiplexing and Binary Framing
paragraphs: HTTP/2, published in 2015, addressed HTTP/1.1's performance limits while maintaining semantic compatibility. The key innovation is multiplexing: many request-response streams share a single TCP connection simultaneously. Streams are independent—slow Stream A doesn't block Stream B. Data is split into binary frames tagged with stream IDs, enabling efficient parsing and eliminating the need for multiple parallel connections.

HTTP/2 also introduced header compression (HPACK), server push (server proactively sends resources), and stream prioritization. In practice, server push saw limited adoption (browsers deprecated it) because preload hints and HTTP caching proved more effective. Header compression, however, is significant—API requests with large JWT tokens or cookie headers benefit substantially.

The critical limitation HTTP/2 didn't solve: TCP-level head-of-line blocking. TCP guarantees ordered byte delivery. If one packet is lost, all subsequent packets on that connection stall until retransmission completes—even if they belong to different HTTP/2 streams. On lossy networks (mobile, cross-continent), this can negate HTTP/2's multiplexing benefits. This limitation directly motivated HTTP/3.

Single TCP connection per origin reduces handshake overhead and memory
Flow control at both connection and stream levels prevents receiver overwhelm

concepts: HTTP methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (update), DELETE (remove)
Status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
HTTP/1.1 keep-alive: persistent connections; head-of-line blocking per connection

Caching: Cache-Control, ETag, If-None-Match, 304 Not Modified, CDN edge caching

Set Cache-Control headers deliberately; use CDN cache tags for granular invalidation
Enable HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 at your CDN/load balancer; fall back gracefully for older clients
Compress responses with gzip or brotli; brotli achieves 15–20% better compression
Implement rate limiting with 429 and Retry-After; use idempotency keys for POST retries
Terminate TLS at the edge (CDN/ALB) and use HTTP/2 for backend connections where possible

examples.title: Shopify's HTTP/3 Rollout
examples.description: Shopify enabled HTTP/3 via QUIC on their CDN, reducing connection setup time for mobile shoppers by ~200ms. They implemented Alt-Svc headers for gradual client migration and maintained HTTP/2 fallback. Checkout completion rates improved measurably on high-latency mobile networks where TCP head-of-line blocking was most severe.

examples.title: Stripe API Idempotency Keys
examples.description: Stripe's POST /v1/charges accepts an Idempotency-Key header. If a client retries due to a network timeout, the same key returns the original response without double-charging. This pattern—essential for any payment or order API—relies on understanding that HTTP POST is not idempotent and network failures are inevitable.

examples.title: GitHub API Conditional Requests
examples.description: GitHub's REST API returns ETag headers on resources. Clients store the ETag and send If-None-Match on subsequent requests. If the resource hasn't changed, GitHub returns 304 with no body—saving bandwidth and processing. Integrations polling GitHub for changes reduced API call volume by 80% using this pattern.

HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection but still suffers TCP-level packet loss blocking
HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves transport-level blocking with independent UDP streams and faster handshakes
Caching with Cache-Control and ETags is the highest-ROI HTTP performance optimization
Correct status codes, methods, and idempotency design are signs of production-grade APIs
Terminate TLS at the edge; use CDNs for static content and cacheable API responses
Always implement graceful fallback across HTTP versions for compatibility
lessons.whyItMatters: HTTP is the lingua franca of web APIs and the protocol your users' browsers speak. Performance tuning, caching strategy, CDN configuration, and API contract design all depend on understanding HTTP semantics and how each version handles connections. In interviews, you'll be asked to design REST APIs, optimize latency, and choose between HTTP and alternatives—this knowledge is the foundation.

How would you design cache invalidation for a product catalog that updates hourly but must never serve stale prices?
When is returning 202 Accepted preferable to 200 OK for a POST endpoint?
Why might an enterprise client behind a strict firewall fail to use HTTP/3, and how would you detect this?
