expert.title: Scheduling & Virtual Memory — Expert Notes
paragraphs: Expert considerations for Scheduling & Virtual Memory: multi-region behavior, cost envelopes, and edge cases under overload.

concepts: Preemptive scheduling: OS interrupts tasks via timer and priority
CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler): Linux default, vruntime-based fairness
Nice value and cgroup CPU quota: influence CPU share in containers
Virtual address space vs physical RAM: MMU translation via page tables
Page fault: soft (demand alloc) vs major (disk I/O required)
TLB: cache for virtual-to-physical translations
Swap: evict cold pages to disk, major fault on re-access
OOM killer: reclaims memory by terminating processes
Copy-on-write: fork shares pages until write
Working set: pages actively used — keep this in RAM for performance
practices: Monitor major page faults and swap usage — non-zero swap on a database node is a red flag
Set Kubernetes memory requests to expected working set; limits high enough to avoid OOM during spikes but low enough to prevent node exhaustion
Use huge pages for large, long-lived allocations (database buffer pools) to reduce TLB misses
Separate latency-sensitive and batch workloads onto different nodes or QoS tiers
Profile GC and allocator behavior under load — virtual memory freed != physical memory returned
Size RAM as working set + 20–30% headroom; never run memory-heavy services without limits
Understand NUMA topology on bare metal — pin memory and CPU for HPC and large in-memory stores
pitfalls: Assuming free memory is wasted memory — Linux uses spare RAM for page cache, which speeds reads
Setting JVM heap close to container limit without accounting for off-heap, threads, and metaspace
Ignoring load average > core count sustained — indicates runnable queue backlog
Running swap enabled on database or cache servers — masks memory pressure until catastrophic latency
Overcommitting node memory (sum of pod limits >> node RAM) — guarantees OOM under pressure
Confusing virtual size (VSZ) with resident set (RSS) when debugging memory leaks

examples.title: PostgreSQL and shared_buffers
examples.description: PostgreSQL allocates shared_buffers (often 25% of RAM) as a buffer pool for page caching. The OS page cache holds additional copies of recently read data. If the machine swaps, both pools compete for scarce RAM and query latency spikes on buffer cache misses that become disk reads. Production tuning starts with ensuring shared_buffers + OS headroom fits in physical memory with swap disabled or minimized.

examples.title: Kubernetes CPU throttling
examples.description: A pod with cpu.limit=500m and a Java app doing GC or compilation bursts gets throttled by CFS quota — the process runs only half of each 100ms period. p99 latency rises even though average CPU looks low. The fix is raising limits, requesting guaranteed QoS, or using dedicated nodes — all scheduling and cgroup decisions, not application bugs.

examples.title: Major page fault in a cold start
examples.description: A serverless function or freshly restarted service maps a large binary and touches many code pages on first requests. Each cold page causes a soft fault loading from disk. Warm instances keep pages resident. This is why 'cold start latency' is a memory and paging phenomenon as much as initialization logic — and why provisioned concurrency or keeping instances warm helps.

keyTakeaways: The scheduler balances fairness, throughput, and latency via preemptive time slicing
Virtual memory isolates processes and enables demand paging, but page faults cost time
Swapping moves cold pages to disk — fine for idle desktops, deadly for databases
OOM killer and cgroup limits are safety valves when physical memory is exhausted
Working set size drives RAM provisioning — measure RSS and page fault rates, not just heap settings
Container CPU/memory limits are OS scheduling and cgroup mechanisms — understand them when tuning
TLB and huge pages matter at scale for in-memory and database workloads
lessons.whyItMatters: Capacity planning, container sizing, database tuning, and latency debugging all require understanding what happens when RAM runs out and how the CPU chooses what runs next. 'We need more CPUs' is often wrong — the runnable queue is empty but threads block on I/O. 'We need an index' is sometimes wrong — the working set exceeded RAM and the system swapped. Scheduling and virtual memory are the lens for these diagnoses.
reflectionQuestions: Your PostgreSQL node's swap usage is 2 GB and query p99 jumped 10×. Walk through what the kernel is doing and your remediation steps.
A pod is OOMKilled repeatedly with a 1 GB limit. The app owner says 'the heap is only 512 MB.' What else consumes memory in a JVM or Node process?
How would you isolate a batch ETL job from a payment API on the same Kubernetes cluster?
Explain why load average of 8 on a 4-core machine indicates a problem even if CPU utilization shows 50%.

lessons.title: Chunking, Hybrid Search & Reranking
lessons.summary: RAG quality is dominated by retrieval design: how you chunk, what you index, how you fuse lexical and dense signals, and how you rerank before generation.

sections.title: Chunking is an API contract
paragraphs: Chunk size, overlap, and metadata (title, section path, ACLs, timestamps) determine what the model can cite. Over-long chunks dilute embeddings; over-short chunks lose context. Structure-aware chunking (headings, tables) usually beats fixed character windows.

sections.title: Hybrid retrieval and reranking
paragraphs: Lexical search (BM25) handles rare identifiers; dense vectors handle paraphrase. Fuse candidates (e.g. reciprocal rank fusion) then apply a cross-encoder or LLM reranker on a shortlist. Always enforce document ACLs before the prompt is built.

lessons.title: Retries, Circuit Breakers & Backpressure
lessons.summary: Production systems fail constantly — networks blip, dependencies slow down, disks fill up. Reliability patterns prevent small failures from cascading into outages. Retries recover transient errors, circuit breakers stop calling broken services, bulkheads isolate blast radius, and backpressure prevents overload.

sections.title: Designing for Failure
paragraphs: Every dependency will fail eventually: databases, payment gateways, third-party APIs, DNS, the network itself. Reliability engineering assumes failure is normal and designs systems to degrade gracefully rather than collapse entirely.

The goal is not zero failures — it is bounded impact, fast recovery, and predictable degradation. Users may see slower responses or reduced features, but the core service stays available. SLOs (Service Level Objectives) define acceptable failure budgets.

Reliability patterns are implemented in application code, client libraries (gRPC retries), service meshes (Istio circuit breaking), and infrastructure (load shedder, rate limiters). Consistency across services matters — one service without timeouts can hang an entire call chain.

sections.title: Retries, Timeouts, and Jitter
paragraphs: Retries recover from transient failures: network timeouts, 503 responses, connection resets. Always combine retries with timeouts — a retry without a timeout can wait forever. Set deadlines per request and per call chain.

Exponential backoff increases delay between retries (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) to give failing services time to recover. Jitter adds randomness to prevent synchronized retry storms — without jitter, thousands of clients retry simultaneously and re-overwhelm the recovering service.

Retry only idempotent operations unless using idempotency keys. POST /charge without an idempotency key must not blind retry — you may double-charge. GET, PUT with idempotency keys, and DELETE are safer retry candidates.

sections.title: Circuit Breakers
paragraphs: A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failure rates. Closed (normal): calls pass through. Open (tripped): calls fail fast without hitting the dependency — return fallback or error immediately. Half-open: allow a probe request to test recovery.

Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures. When the payment service is down, the order service stops hammering it, returns a graceful error, and preserves threads and connection pools for healthy paths.
Netflix Hystrix popularized this pattern; today Resilience4j, Polly, and service meshes provide implementations. Configure failure thresholds, reset timeouts, and fallbacks per dependency.

sections.title: Bulkheads, Rate Limiting, and Load Shedding
paragraphs: Bulkheads isolate resources — separate thread pools or connection pools per dependency so one slow service cannot exhaust all threads. Named after ship compartments that contain flooding.

Rate limiting protects services from overload: token bucket and sliding window algorithms cap requests per client or globally. Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header. Rate limit at the edge (API gateway) and at critical internal services.

Load shedding drops requests when the system is overloaded — prefer rejecting new work over failing all in-flight requests. Prioritize critical paths (checkout) over background jobs (recommendations).

sections.title: Backpressure
paragraphs: Backpressure signals upstream producers to slow down when downstream consumers cannot keep pace. Without backpressure, buffers grow unbounded until memory exhaustion — the slow consumer problem.
Reactive streams (Project Reactor, RxJava), gRPC flow control, and Kafka consumer pause/resume implement backpressure. TCP itself applies backpressure via window sizes.
In queue-based systems, monitor queue depth and scale consumers or throttle producers when depth exceeds thresholds. Unbounded queues are a reliability anti-pattern.

paragraphs: Bulkheads isolate resources — separate thread pools or connection pools per dependency so one slow service cannot exhaust all threads. Named after ship compartments that contain flooding.

Rate limiting protects services from overload: token bucket and sliding window algorithms cap requests per client or globally. Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header. Rate limit at the edge (API gateway) and at critical internal services.

Load shedding drops requests when the system is overloaded — prefer rejecting new work over failing all in-flight requests. Prioritize critical paths (checkout) over background jobs (recommendations).

core.title: Backpressure
paragraphs: Backpressure signals upstream producers to slow down when downstream consumers cannot keep pace. Without backpressure, buffers grow unbounded until memory exhaustion — the slow consumer problem.
Reactive streams (Project Reactor, RxJava), gRPC flow control, and Kafka consumer pause/resume implement backpressure. TCP itself applies backpressure via window sizes.
In queue-based systems, monitor queue depth and scale consumers or throttle producers when depth exceeds thresholds. Unbounded queues are a reliability anti-pattern.

examples.title: Payment service circuit breaker
examples.description: Order service wraps payment API calls in a circuit breaker. After 5 failures in 10 seconds, circuit opens — orders queue for later payment retry and users see 'payment processing.' Half-open after 30 seconds probes one request. Success closes circuit; failure reopens.

examples.title: Retry storm without jitter
examples.description: A DNS blip causes 500 errors. Ten thousand clients retry simultaneously every second with fixed 1s backoff. The recovering service is immediately overwhelmed again. Adding full jitter spreads retries over a window, allowing recovery.

examples.title: Kafka backpressure
examples.description: A consumer processing messages slower than production rate accumulates lag. Consumer pauses partition fetching when internal buffer is full — applying backpressure to the broker. Alert fires on lag > 100K; autoscaler adds consumer instances.

Retries need backoff, jitter, timeouts, and idempotency
Circuit breakers fail fast and prevent cascade overload
Bulkheads and rate limits contain blast radius
Backpressure prevents unbounded buffering and OOM
Test failure modes — reliability patterns must be verified under chaos

These patterns are the difference between a blip and a multi-hour incident. They appear in every system design discussion about production readiness.

lessons.title: Stateless Services & State Management
lessons.summary: Stateless services can be added, removed, and replaced freely — they are the foundation of elastic, fault-tolerant systems. State must be deliberately placed in databases, caches, message queues, or object stores. Misplaced state is the most common reason scaling efforts fail.

sections.title: Stateless vs Stateful Services
paragraphs: A stateless service treats every request independently. It does not rely on data stored in local memory from a previous request on the same machine. Any instance can handle any request. This property enables horizontal scaling, rolling deployments, and instant recovery from node failure.

A stateful service remembers context across requests or over time — in-memory session stores, local file caches, embedded databases, or workflow state tied to a specific process. Stateful services require sticky routing, replication, or leader election to scale and survive failures.

Most production architectures push toward stateless application tiers while concentrating state in specialized, managed stores. The application becomes a thin orchestration layer: validate input, read/write state externally, return a response.

sections.title: Where State Should Live
paragraphs: User sessions belong in a distributed cache (Redis, Memcached) or a database — not in JVM heap or Node.js process memory. Redis offers TTL-based expiry, atomic operations, and sub-millisecond latency, making it the default session store for scaled web apps.

Long-lived domain data lives in the primary database with ACID guarantees. Caches hold derived or hot data with explicit invalidation policies. Workflow and job state goes to durable queues or workflow engines (Temporal, Step Functions). Uploaded files go to object storage (S3), not local disk.

Configuration and secrets belong in environment variables, config services, or secrets managers — injected at startup, not baked into images. Feature flags live in dedicated flag services so behavior can change without redeployment.
bullets: Session state → Redis / DynamoDB with TTL
Domain data → PostgreSQL / MySQL / distributed DB
Ephemeral hot data → in-memory cache with eviction policy
Async work state → message queues or workflow engines

sections.title: Sticky Sessions and Their Trade-offs
paragraphs: Sticky sessions (session affinity) route a user to the same server using cookies or load balancer rules. They allow in-memory session storage without immediate externalization — a tempting shortcut during early development.

The downsides are significant. Uneven load distribution occurs when some users are heavier than others. Node failure drops all sessions pinned to that node unless sessions are replicated (which reintroduces complexity). Rolling deployments require draining sticky connections carefully.

Sticky sessions are acceptable for WebSocket connections where connection state is inherently tied to a node — but even then, teams use pub/sub backplanes (Redis) to broadcast messages across a cluster. For HTTP APIs, prefer external session stores over stickiness.

sections.title: Shared-Nothing Architecture
paragraphs: Shared-nothing means each node is self-sufficient: own CPU, memory, and local disk, with no shared memory or filesystem between application servers. Nodes communicate only through the network via databases, caches, and queues.

This model maximizes fault isolation. One node's crash does not corrupt another's memory. Scaling is linear: add nodes, update load balancer, done. Google's Bigtable, Cassandra, and most microservice deployments follow shared-nothing principles.

The trade-off is network round-trips for every state access. Poorly designed systems chatter excessively with Redis and the database. Connection pooling, batching, and local caching (with short TTLs) mitigate latency while preserving statelessness at the service level.

examples.title: JWT vs server-side sessions
examples.description: A mobile API uses signed JWTs for authentication — no server-side session store needed, enabling fully stateless API gateways. A web app with instant logout requirements uses Redis sessions instead, because JWTs cannot be revoked without a blocklist (which reintroduces state).

examples.title: Shopping cart during peak traffic
examples.description: Cart state lives in Redis keyed by user ID with a 7-day TTL. API servers are interchangeable. During a node failure, users retry and hit a different server — cart data is intact. Checkout transitions cart to an order in PostgreSQL atomically.

keyTakeaways: Stateless application tiers are prerequisite for elastic horizontal scaling
Every piece of state needs an explicit, durable home — never accidental local memory
Sticky sessions are a bridge, not a destination; externalize sessions for resilience
Shared-nothing architecture isolates failures and simplifies scaling
Choose JWT for stateless auth; server-side sessions when revocation matters
Kill nodes in testing to verify your state management actually works

lessons.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
lessons.summary: Scaling is how systems handle growth in traffic, data, and complexity. Vertical scaling adds power to a single machine; horizontal scaling adds more machines. Production architectures almost always combine both, but horizontal scaling — with stateless services and load balancing — is the path to massive, fault-tolerant scale.

sections.title: What Scaling Means in Practice
paragraphs: When users, requests, or data volume grow, every component in your stack faces pressure: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network bandwidth, and connection limits. Scaling is the set of strategies you use to increase capacity without rewriting the entire system.

The two fundamental approaches are vertical scaling (scale up) and horizontal scaling (scale out). Vertical scaling means upgrading the hardware or instance size of a single node — more cores, more RAM, faster SSDs. Horizontal scaling means running multiple copies of a service behind a load balancer and distributing work across them.

Early-stage products often scale vertically because it requires no architectural changes: you resize the database instance or upgrade the app server. But vertical scaling has hard ceilings — single-machine limits, diminishing returns on cost, and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling removes those ceilings but demands that your application, data layer, and deployment pipeline support distribution from the start or through deliberate refactoring.

sections.title: Vertical Scaling: Strengths and Limits
paragraphs: Vertical scaling is operationally simple. You change an instance type, restart services, and capacity increases. Databases especially benefit early on: a larger PostgreSQL instance with more RAM holds more of the working set in memory, reducing disk reads dramatically.

The limits appear quickly at scale. Cloud providers cap instance sizes; beyond a certain point, doubling RAM costs more than doubling throughput. A single large database cannot survive zone failures without replication. Memory-bound workloads may not fit on any commercially available machine.

Vertical scaling also creates upgrade windows: migrating from db.r5.2xlarge to db.r5.4xlarge often requires downtime or complex failover. Teams that rely exclusively on vertical scaling eventually hit a wall where the only option is a painful horizontal split — sharding, read replicas, or service extraction.
bullets: Best for: early growth, stateful monoliths, workloads that resist distribution
Watch for: cost curves that outpace revenue, single points of failure, upgrade downtime

sections.title: Horizontal Scaling: Architecture Requirements
paragraphs: Horizontal scaling distributes load across N identical nodes. A load balancer — L4 (TCP) or L7 (HTTP) — routes incoming requests using algorithms like round-robin, least connections, or consistent hashing. Health checks remove unhealthy nodes automatically.

For horizontal scaling to work, application servers must be stateless or share state through external stores. Session data in local memory breaks horizontal scale: killing one node loses sessions for users pinned to it. Externalize sessions to Redis, use JWTs, or accept sticky sessions with their trade-offs.

Data layers scale horizontally through read replicas (scale reads), sharding (partition writes across nodes), or purpose-built distributed databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB). Each approach introduces consistency, query, and operational complexity that vertical scaling avoided.

sections.title: Auto-Scaling and Elastic Capacity
paragraphs: Modern cloud platforms offer auto-scaling groups that add or remove instances based on metrics — CPU utilization, request rate, queue depth, or custom CloudWatch/Prometheus signals. Elastic capacity matches cost to demand: fewer servers at 3 AM, more during peak events.

Auto-scaling requires warm-up time. New instances must pass health checks, load application code, and establish connection pools before accepting traffic. Scale-out policies should trigger before saturation; scale-in policies should be conservative to avoid flapping during variable load.

Design for scale-to-zero only when cold-start latency is acceptable (serverless functions). For latency-sensitive APIs, maintain a minimum fleet size and use predictive scaling for known traffic patterns like product launches or Black Friday.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Strategy
paragraphs: Start vertical when the team is small and traffic is predictable. Plan horizontal paths before you need them: stateless services, connection pooling, database read replicas, and clear service boundaries make future scale-out feasible.

Use vertical scaling for components that are inherently hard to distribute — single-leader databases, legacy monoliths, or licensed software with per-core pricing. Use horizontal scaling for stateless APIs, worker pools, CDN edges, and stream processors.

The best production systems combine both: vertically sized database primaries with horizontally scaled read replicas; horizontally scaled API tiers on moderately sized instances rather than one giant machine or hundreds of tiny ones.

examples.title: E-commerce checkout API
examples.description: An checkout service runs as 20 stateless containers behind an ALB. Session carts live in Redis; orders write to a PostgreSQL primary with two read replicas for order history. During flash sales, auto-scaling adds API containers from 20 to 80 based on request count, while the database scales vertically once before adding read replicas.

examples.title: Video transcoding pipeline
examples.description: Transcoding is embarrassingly parallel: each video chunk is independent. A job queue (SQS) feeds a horizontally scaled worker fleet. Workers scale from 5 to 500 based on queue depth. No vertical scaling needed — each worker is a modest CPU-optimized instance.

examples.title: Legacy monolith migration path

Combine vertical and horizontal strategies per component — one size does not fit all
Identify bottlenecks with load tests before scaling the wrong layer
Plan horizontal paths early even if you scale vertically today

lessons.title: Authentication, Authorization & Encryption
lessons.summary: Security is layered defense: verify identity (authentication), enforce permissions (authorization), protect data in transit and at rest (encryption), and manage secrets safely. Most breaches stem from misconfigured auth, leaked credentials, and missing encryption — not sophisticated zero-day exploits.

sections.title: Authentication: Proving Identity
paragraphs: Authentication answers 'who are you?' Common mechanisms include username/password (with bcrypt/argon2 hashing), multi-factor authentication (TOTP, WebAuthn), API keys, and federated identity via OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC).

OAuth 2.0 delegates authorization to an identity provider (Google, Okta, Auth0) without sharing passwords. OIDC adds an identity layer — ID tokens (JWTs) containing user claims. The authorization code flow with PKCE is the standard for web and mobile apps.

JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) encode claims in a signed, base64 payload. Stateless verification is fast — no server-side session lookup. Downsides: revocation is hard (requires blocklists or short TTLs), tokens can be stolen if not stored securely, and payload is readable (not encrypted) unless using JWE.

sections.title: Authorization: Enforcing Permissions
paragraphs: Authorization answers 'what can you do?' Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) assigns permissions to roles (admin, editor, viewer) and roles to users. Simple and widely used for internal tools and SaaS products.

Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) evaluates policies against attributes — user department, resource owner, time of day, IP range. More flexible for complex enterprise policies. Policy engines (OPA, Cedar) evaluate ABAC rules at runtime.

Principle of least privilege: grant minimum permissions needed. Service accounts for machine-to-machine auth get scoped API keys or mTLS certificates — never root credentials. Regularly audit and rotate permissions.

sections.title: Encryption in Transit and at Rest
paragraphs: Encryption in transit protects data on the wire via TLS 1.2+ (HTTPS, mTLS for service-to-service). Terminate TLS at the load balancer or service mesh; enforce HSTS and modern cipher suites. Never transmit secrets or PII over unencrypted HTTP.

Encryption at rest protects stored data: database TDE (Transparent Data Encryption), S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS), disk encryption on VMs. Keys managed by KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) with rotation policies.

Application-level encryption adds a layer for especially sensitive fields (SSN, credit card) — encrypt before storing so a database breach does not expose plaintext. Manage field-level keys separately from storage keys.

sections.title: Secrets Management
paragraphs: Secrets — API keys, database passwords, TLS private keys, encryption keys — must never appear in source code, Docker images, or git history. Use secrets managers: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, GCP Secret Manager, Kubernetes Secrets (with encryption at rest enabled).
Inject secrets at runtime via environment variables or mounted volumes. Rotate secrets automatically where supported. Audit access to secrets — who read which secret when.
Development environments use separate secrets from production. .env files are for local dev only — add to .gitignore and use tools like git-secrets to prevent accidental commits.

sections.title: Security in System Design
paragraphs: Defense in depth: WAF at the edge, network segmentation (VPCs, security groups), auth at API gateway, authorization in services, encryption everywhere. No single layer is sufficient.

Input validation and parameterized queries prevent injection attacks. Rate limiting and CAPTCHA mitigate brute force. Security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options) reduce browser-side attacks. Log and alert on auth failures and privilege escalation attempts.

Compliance frameworks (SOC 2, GDPR, PCI-DSS) mandate specific controls — understand which apply to your domain. Security is a continuous process: dependency scanning, penetration testing, and incident response plans.

examples.title: SaaS multi-tenant authorization
examples.description: Users authenticate via Auth0 (OIDC). JWT contains user_id and org_id. API middleware extracts claims; each query filters by org_id for tenant isolation. Admin role checked via RBAC policy engine (OPA). Cross-tenant access returns 403.

examples.title: Microservice mTLS mesh
examples.description: Services in a Kubernetes cluster communicate via Istio service mesh with mutual TLS. Each service has a SPIFFE identity certificate. Unauthorized services cannot call internal APIs even if they reach the network — identity is verified on every request.

examples.title: PCI-compliant payment handling
examples.description: Credit card data never touches application servers — Stripe Elements tokenizes on the client. Tokens are sent to the backend, which calls Stripe API over TLS. Database stores only last-four digits. Secrets (Stripe API key) live in AWS Secrets Manager with 90-day rotation.

Authorize at every layer — gateway and service level
Encrypt in transit (TLS) and at rest (KMS) by default
Secrets belong in secrets managers, never in code or images
JWTs enable stateless auth but complicate revocation — use short TTLs
Least privilege for users and service accounts limits breach impact

lessons.title: Essential Design Patterns
lessons.summary: Design patterns are reusable solutions to recurring problems in software architecture — not copy-paste recipes, but a shared vocabulary for discussing trade-offs. This lesson covers the patterns that appear most often in production systems and system design interviews: creational patterns for object lifecycle, structural patterns for composition, and behavioral patterns for communication and responsibility.

sections.title: Why Patterns Matter in System Design
paragraphs: A design pattern names a problem-solution pair that experienced engineers recognize instantly. When someone says 'we used a circuit breaker here' or 'this is a classic observer setup,' the entire team understands the constraints, failure modes, and alternatives without a whiteboard session from scratch.

Patterns sit at the intersection of code and architecture. Singleton and Factory appear in application code; Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, and Saga span service boundaries. Learning patterns trains you to see structural similarities across domains — a payment retry queue and a notification dispatcher both implement variations of the same publish-subscribe and retry idioms.

Patterns are not goals. Applying every pattern from the Gang of Four catalog to a simple CRUD app is over-engineering. The skill is recognizing when a recurring force — varying object creation, decoupling senders from receivers, isolating failure domains — makes a named pattern the simplest correct solution.

In interviews, patterns demonstrate that you think in abstractions transferable across companies and stacks. In production, they give you proven starting points with documented pitfalls, so you spend design time on domain specifics rather than reinventing structural solutions.
bullets: Pattern = recurring problem + context + proven solution + consequences
GoF (1994): 23 classic OOP patterns — still relevant at architectural scale
Enterprise patterns (Fowler, Hohpe): messaging, integration, domain logic
Cloud-native patterns: sidecar, ambassador, anti-corruption layer

sections.title: Creational Patterns: Controlling Object Creation
paragraphs: Creational patterns manage how objects are instantiated — critical when construction is expensive, configuration varies, or you need to enforce a single shared instance. Factory Method and Abstract Factory delegate creation to subclasses or factory objects, letting you swap implementations (PostgreSQL vs. DynamoDB repository) without changing callers.

Builder separates construction of a complex object from its representation. You see this in fluent API clients (AWS SDK builders), SQL query builders, and HTTP request construction. It prevents telescoping constructors with twelve optional parameters and makes immutable objects practical.

Singleton guarantees one instance — useful for connection pool managers, configuration registries, and metric collectors. The danger is hidden global state: singletons make testing hard, create hidden coupling, and in distributed systems, 'singleton' is a lie unless backed by leader election. Prefer dependency injection with a scoped lifetime over static singletons in modern codebases.

Prototype clones existing objects instead of building from scratch — valuable when object creation requires parsing configs or deep copying is cheaper than re-fetching. Object pools (borrow/return instead of new/GC) are creational cousins common in database drivers and thread pools.
bullets: Factory Method: subclass decides which concrete type to instantiate
Abstract Factory: families of related objects (UI toolkit, storage backend)
Builder: step-by-step construction with validation at build() time
Singleton: one instance — use sparingly; prefer DI container scoping

sections.title: Structural Patterns: Composition and Adaptation
paragraphs: Structural patterns organize classes and objects into larger structures while keeping them flexible and efficient. Adapter wraps an incompatible interface so legacy code works with new APIs — the classic integration pattern when you cannot rewrite the vendor SDK or third-party service.

Decorator adds behavior dynamically without subclass explosion. Middleware stacks in Express, Koa, and gRPC interceptors are decorator chains: logging wraps auth wraps rate limiting wraps the handler. Each layer implements the same interface and delegates to the inner layer.

Facade provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem. An API gateway is a distributed facade: clients call one endpoint; the gateway routes to dozens of internal services. Inside a monolith, a service layer facade hides repository, cache, and messaging details from controllers.

Proxy controls access to another object — lazy loading, access control, caching, or remote calls. Smart references in ORMs that lazy-load associations, caching proxies in Redis clients, and RPC stubs are all proxies. Composite treats individual objects and groups uniformly — useful for tree structures like org charts, file systems, and UI component trees.
bullets: Adapter: translate one interface to another (legacy integration)
Decorator: stack behaviors without modifying original class
Facade: single entry point hiding subsystem complexity
Proxy: indirection for lazy load, cache, security, or remote access

sections.title: Behavioral Patterns: Communication and Responsibility
paragraphs: Behavioral patterns govern how objects interact and distribute responsibility. Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when one object changes state, dependents are notified. Event buses, WebSocket push, React state updates, and domain event publishing are observer variants at different scales.

Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms. Payment processing (credit card vs. PayPal vs. crypto), compression codecs, and routing algorithms all use strategy so runtime configuration swaps behavior without conditional spaghetti. Dependency injection makes strategy trivial — inject the interface, not the implementation.

Command encapsulates a request as an object, enabling undo, queuing, logging, and retry. Job queues (Sidekiq, SQS consumers) process command objects. CQRS command handlers are named commands with idempotent execution. Template Method defines a skeleton algorithm with overridable steps — base class handles the flow, subclasses fill in specifics.

Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a handler chain until someone processes it — middleware pipelines, servlet filters, and approval workflows. State pattern lets an object alter behavior when its internal state changes — order lifecycle (pending → paid → shipped) without giant switch statements.
bullets: Observer: publish-subscribe within and across process boundaries
Strategy: swap algorithms at runtime via interface injection
Command: requests as first-class objects — queue, log, undo, retry
Chain of Responsibility: middleware and filter pipelines

sections.title: Patterns at Architectural Scale
paragraphs: Many 'microservice patterns' are behavioral and structural patterns scaled to the network. Circuit Breaker (from Release It!) stops calling a failing dependency after a threshold, failing fast instead of hanging threads. Bulkhead isolates thread pools or connection pools so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all resources.

Saga coordinates long-running distributed transactions through a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions — the distributed cousin of Command + undo. Outbox pattern combines Observer with transactional integrity: write events to a database table in the same transaction as business data, then a relay publishes to Kafka.

Anti-Corruption Layer (from DDD) is an Adapter at bounded-context boundaries — translate external models into your domain language so legacy systems do not leak their terminology into your core model. Sidecar and Ambassador (from cloud-native patterns) attach cross-cutting concerns (logging, TLS, retries) without polluting application code.

The meta-pattern: choose the pattern that minimizes the cost of the change you expect. If algorithms vary, use Strategy. If wiring varies, use Factory. If failure isolation matters, use Bulkhead and Circuit Breaker. Name your choices so the next engineer understands intent.

paragraphs: Behavioral patterns govern how objects interact and distribute responsibility. Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when one object changes state, dependents are notified. Event buses, WebSocket push, React state updates, and domain event publishing are observer variants at different scales.

Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms. Payment processing (credit card vs. PayPal vs. crypto), compression codecs, and routing algorithms all use strategy so runtime configuration swaps behavior without conditional spaghetti. Dependency injection makes strategy trivial — inject the interface, not the implementation.

Command encapsulates a request as an object, enabling undo, queuing, logging, and retry. Job queues (Sidekiq, SQS consumers) process command objects. CQRS command handlers are named commands with idempotent execution. Template Method defines a skeleton algorithm with overridable steps — base class handles the flow, subclasses fill in specifics.

Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a handler chain until someone processes it — middleware pipelines, servlet filters, and approval workflows. State pattern lets an object alter behavior when its internal state changes — order lifecycle (pending → paid → shipped) without giant switch statements.
bullets: Observer: publish-subscribe within and across process boundaries
Strategy: swap algorithms at runtime via interface injection
Command: requests as first-class objects — queue, log, undo, retry
Chain of Responsibility: middleware and filter pipelines

core.title: Patterns at Architectural Scale
paragraphs: Many 'microservice patterns' are behavioral and structural patterns scaled to the network. Circuit Breaker (from Release It!) stops calling a failing dependency after a threshold, failing fast instead of hanging threads. Bulkhead isolates thread pools or connection pools so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all resources.

Saga coordinates long-running distributed transactions through a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions — the distributed cousin of Command + undo. Outbox pattern combines Observer with transactional integrity: write events to a database table in the same transaction as business data, then a relay publishes to Kafka.

Anti-Corruption Layer (from DDD) is an Adapter at bounded-context boundaries — translate external models into your domain language so legacy systems do not leak their terminology into your core model. Sidecar and Ambassador (from cloud-native patterns) attach cross-cutting concerns (logging, TLS, retries) without polluting application code.

The meta-pattern: choose the pattern that minimizes the cost of the change you expect. If algorithms vary, use Strategy. If wiring varies, use Factory. If failure isolation matters, use Bulkhead and Circuit Breaker. Name your choices so the next engineer understands intent.

expert.title: Essential Design Patterns — Expert Notes

concepts: Factory Method / Abstract Factory: delegate creation to swap implementations
Builder: construct complex objects step-by-step with validation
Singleton: single instance — global state risk in tests and distributed systems
Adapter: wrap incompatible interfaces for integration
Decorator: add behavior via composable wrapper chains (middleware)
Observer: one-to-many notification — events, pub/sub, reactive UI
Strategy: interchangeable algorithms selected at runtime
Command: encapsulate requests for queue, retry, undo, audit
Circuit Breaker: fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy
Saga: distributed transaction via compensating local steps
practices: Name patterns in design docs so reviewers instantly grasp structure and trade-offs
Prefer composition (Decorator, Strategy) over deep inheritance hierarchies
Use Factory or DI to swap implementations — never hard-code concrete types in business logic
Apply Circuit Breaker and Bulkhead on every synchronous cross-service call
Replace switch-on-type with Strategy or polymorphism when behavior varies by category
Use Command objects for async work — enables retry, idempotency keys, and dead letter queues
Avoid Singleton for testability; inject shared instances through your DI container
pitfalls: Pattern obsession: adding indirection when a simple function or module suffices
Singleton abuse: hidden global state, untestable code, false 'single instance' in distributed systems
Wrong pattern for the force: using Observer when polling or batch processing is simpler
Leaky abstraction: Decorator chains so deep that debugging requires tracing ten layers
Ignoring consequences: Saga compensations are hard — not every workflow fits choreographed events
Copy-paste from tutorials without adapting to domain constraints and failure modes

examples.title: Express middleware as Decorator chain
examples.description: An Express app stacks middleware functions — each implements (req, res, next), adds behavior (auth check, body parsing, logging), and calls next(). The final route handler sits at the innermost layer. Adding rate limiting means inserting a new decorator without touching existing handlers.

examples.title: Netflix Hystrix → Resilience4j Circuit Breaker
examples.description: When a downstream recommendation service latency spikes, the circuit breaker opens after error/latency thresholds. Callers receive fallback responses immediately instead of blocking threads. After a cooldown, half-open probes test recovery. This is the Circuit Breaker pattern applied at service mesh scale.

examples.title: E-commerce order Saga
examples.description: PlaceOrder → ReserveInventory → ChargePayment → ShipOrder. If payment fails after inventory reservation, a compensating ReleaseInventory command runs. Each step is a local transaction; the saga coordinator (or choreographed events) ensures the workflow completes or rolls back logically — not via a single distributed lock.

keyTakeaways: Patterns are a shared vocabulary for proven solutions to recurring design forces
Creational patterns control object lifecycle; structural patterns organize composition; behavioral patterns govern interaction
Middleware, event buses, and job queues are production-scale Command, Decorator, and Observer
Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, and Saga are essential architectural patterns for distributed systems
Choose patterns based on expected change — not to fill a catalog checklist
Every pattern has consequences; name them in design reviews so trade-offs stay visible
Dependency injection makes Strategy, Factory, and test doubles natural in modern codebases
lessons.whyItMatters: Senior engineers communicate design intent in pattern names and apply proven structures instead of reinventing fragile ad-hoc solutions. In interviews and architecture reviews, recognizing patterns — and knowing when not to use them — signals maturity and saves teams months of debugging implicit design decisions.
reflectionQuestions: Identify three patterns in a codebase you know. For each, what problem force does it address, and what are its consequences?
When would you choose a Saga over a two-phase commit? What compensating actions would an order cancellation require?
Draw the middleware chain for an HTTP request in your stack. Which layers are Decorator, which are Chain of Responsibility?
Where have you seen Singleton cause testing or scaling problems? What would you use instead?

lessons.title: SQL, NoSQL & Specialized Storage
lessons.summary: Different data shapes, access patterns, and consistency requirements demand different storage engines. Modern systems use polyglot persistence — SQL for transactional records, document stores for flexible schemas, key-value for speed, column-family for write-heavy workloads, time-series for metrics, and object storage for blobs.

sections.title: Relational Databases (SQL)
paragraphs: Relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server) store data in tables with defined schemas, relationships, and constraints. SQL provides a powerful query language for joins, aggregations, filtering, and transactions spanning multiple rows.

ACID transactions make relational databases the default for financial records, inventory, user accounts, and any domain where consistency and integrity are non-negotiable. PostgreSQL in particular offers JSON columns, full-text search, and extensions that blur the line with document stores.

Scaling relational databases vertically is straightforward; horizontal scaling requires read replicas, partitioning, or sharding — each adding operational complexity. Schema migrations must be planned carefully in large teams.

sections.title: Document and Key-Value Stores
paragraphs: Document databases (MongoDB, Couchbase) store JSON-like documents with flexible schemas. They excel when entities are self-contained, schema evolves frequently, or nested structures avoid expensive joins. Indexing on nested fields requires thoughtful design.

Key-value stores (Redis, DynamoDB, etcd) optimize for simple get/put/delete by key with predictable latency. Redis adds rich data structures (sorted sets, hashes) and optional persistence. DynamoDB offers managed, partition-key-driven scale with configurable consistency.

Choose document stores when your access pattern is 'fetch entity by ID with all related fields.' Choose key-value when access is strictly by key and you need extreme speed or horizontal scale without joins.

sections.title: Column-Family and Wide-Column Stores
paragraphs: Column-family databases (Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB) organize data by partition key into wide rows with many columns. They optimize for high write throughput, geographic distribution, and time-ordered data within a partition.

Cassandra's tunable consistency and peer-to-peer architecture suit write-heavy workloads: IoT telemetry, activity feeds, messaging metadata. Queries must be designed around partition keys — ad-hoc analytics require separate pipelines.
These stores trade flexible querying for write scalability and availability. They are poor fits for workloads needing multi-row transactions or arbitrary ad-hoc joins.

sections.title: Time-Series and Object Storage
paragraphs: Time-series databases (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, QuestDB) optimize for timestamped metrics: compression, downsampling, retention policies, and time-range queries. They power observability stacks, IoT analytics, and financial tick data.

Object storage (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob) stores unstructured blobs — images, videos, backups, data lake files. It offers durability (11 nines for S3), low cost per GB, and eventual consistency for overwrites. It is not a database: listing, querying, and small-object latency are weak points.
Use time-series DBs for metrics and monitoring data that grows unbounded. Use object storage as the durable, cheap layer for anything that does not need millisecond random access.

sections.title: Polyglot Persistence in Practice
paragraphs: Real systems rarely use one database. An e-commerce platform might use PostgreSQL for orders and users, Redis for carts and rate limiting, Elasticsearch for product search, S3 for product images, and ClickHouse for analytics.

Each store syncs through application code or change-data-capture (CDC) pipelines. The challenge is keeping derived views consistent and handling failures during multi-store writes. Saga patterns and outbox tables help coordinate without distributed transactions across heterogeneous stores.
Choose storage based on access patterns, consistency needs, query flexibility, operational expertise, and cost — not hype. The best database is the one your team can operate reliably.

concepts: ACID transactions: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
SQL relational model: tables, joins, foreign keys, indexes
Document store: flexible schema, nested JSON documents
Key-value store: O(1) lookup by key, partition-key design
Column-family: partition key + clustering columns, write-optimized
Time-series: compression, retention, downsampling, range queries
Object storage: durable blobs, high latency for small objects
Polyglot persistence: multiple specialized stores in one system
CAP/PACELC trade-offs vary by storage engine
Change-data-capture (CDC) for syncing between stores
practices: Model access patterns first, then choose the storage engine
Use PostgreSQL until proven otherwise — it handles most workloads well
Design DynamoDB/Cassandra partition keys to avoid hot partitions
Store files and large blobs in object storage, not database BLOB columns
Define retention and archival policies for time-series and log data
Use read replicas or materialized views for analytics without overloading primary DB
Document which store is source of truth for each entity type
pitfalls: Choosing MongoDB for relational data requiring complex joins and transactions
Storing multi-GB videos in PostgreSQL instead of S3
Hot partition keys in DynamoDB causing throttling on a single shard
Running analytics queries on the production OLTP primary
Assuming eventual consistency is acceptable without defining convergence time
Operating five databases when the team can reliably run one

examples.title: Social media post storage
examples.description: Posts and user profiles live in Cassandra partitioned by user_id for fast timeline writes. Media files upload to S3. Search indexes sync to Elasticsearch via CDC. Follower counts are cached in Redis with periodic reconciliation from Cassandra.

examples.title: SaaS billing platform
examples.description: PostgreSQL holds subscriptions, invoices, and payment records with strict ACID. Stripe webhooks write to an outbox table; a worker publishes events to Kafka. Usage metrics land in TimescaleDB for billing aggregation and dashboards.

keyTakeaways: Match storage to access patterns — there is no universal best database
SQL remains the default for transactional, relational data
NoSQL stores trade query flexibility for scale and schema flexibility
Object storage is for blobs; time-series DBs are for metrics
Polyglot persistence is normal — coordinate with CDC, sagas, and clear ownership
Operational capability matters as much as theoretical performance
lessons.whyItMatters: Storage choice is one of the hardest decisions to reverse. Wrong choices cause performance cliffs, data inconsistency, and runaway costs. Interviewers expect you to justify storage per component, and production systems fail when teams treat all data as rows in one MySQL instance.

Why store images in S3 instead of a database?

lessons.title: Kafka & Nginx Internals
lessons.summary: Kafka and Nginx are infrastructure workhorses — one moves events at scale, the other terminates HTTP at the edge. Kafka's log-structured partitions and consumer groups enable durable, replayable event streams. Nginx's master/worker event-driven model serves millions of connections with minimal memory. Understanding both internals is essential for designing reliable pipelines and high-throughput web tiers.

sections.title: Kafka: Distributed Commit Log Architecture
paragraphs: Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log. Producers append records to topic partitions — ordered, immutable sequences identified by offset. Unlike traditional message queues that delete messages after consumption, Kafka retains records for a configurable period (or size), allowing replay and multiple independent consumer groups.

Each partition is an ordered log stored as segment files on disk (index + .log). Sequential disk writes achieve throughput comparable to memory when batching and page cache cooperate. Partitions are the unit of parallelism: more partitions mean more parallel consumers and producers, up to broker and cluster limits.

Brokers are Kafka server processes. A cluster has many brokers; each partition has one leader broker handling reads/writes and zero or more follower replicas syncing data. ISR (In-Sync Replicas) is the set of followers caught up within a configurable lag. If the leader dies, a follower from ISR is elected — availability and durability depend on replication factor and acks setting.

ZooKeeper (legacy) or KRaft (Kafka Raft metadata mode) manages cluster metadata: broker registration, partition leadership, consumer group offsets (offsets now stored in internal __consumer_offsets topic). KRaft removes the ZooKeeper dependency, simplifying operations in modern Kafka versions.
bullets: Topic → partitions → ordered, append-only log segments
Offset: monotonic position within a partition
Leader + followers; ISR = replicas eligible for leadership
Retention by time (log.retention.hours) or size — not consume-and-delete

sections.title: Kafka: Producers, Consumers, and Delivery Semantics
paragraphs: Producers choose a partition via key hash (same key → same partition → per-key ordering) or round-robin. Batching (linger.ms, batch.size) amortizes network overhead. acks=0 fire-and-forget; acks=1 leader ack; acks=all waits for all ISR — the durability vs latency trade-off.

Consumer groups distribute partitions among group members — each partition consumed by at most one consumer in the group. Rebalance occurs when members join or leave; during rebalance, consumption pauses (unless using cooperative sticky assignors). Scale consumers up to partition count; extra consumers sit idle.

Delivery semantics: at-most-once (commit offset before process — may lose messages), at-least-once (process then commit — may duplicate), exactly-once (Kafka transactions + idempotent producer — higher overhead, limited to Kafka Streams / specific flows). Production systems almost always implement at-least-once with idempotent consumers.

Log compaction retains the latest record per key — useful for changelog topics (KTables, config propagation). Tombstone records (null value) delete keys after delete.retention.ms. Compact + delete retention policies can coexist on different topics.
bullets: Partition key → consistent hashing → per-key ordering guarantee
Consumer group: one consumer per partition within a group
Rebalance: partition reassignment on membership change
Idempotent producer: dedup via PID + sequence number per partition

sections.title: Nginx: Master/Worker and the Event Loop
paragraphs: Nginx uses a master process (reads config, manages workers, binds ports) and one or more worker processes (handle connections). Workers are single-threaded with an event-driven loop — epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD. Thousands of idle connections cost kilobytes each (connection state), not megabytes per thread.

The event loop: register socket events (readable, writable), wait via epoll_wait, dispatch handlers. Non-blocking I/O is mandatory — a blocking read in one worker stalls all connections that worker manages. Proxy upstream calls use the same non-blocking model with retry and timeout logic.

Accept mutex (older versions) or SO_REUSEPORT (modern) distributes incoming connections across workers. SO_REUSEPORT lets each worker bind the same port; the kernel load-balances accepts — better CPU utilization on multi-core hosts.

Static file serving uses sendfile (zero-copy from disk to socket, bypassing user-space buffer copies). gzip/brotli compression, caching headers, and open_file_cache reduce disk and CPU for repeat assets. These optimizations explain why Nginx dominates static content and reverse proxy roles.
bullets: Master/worker: workers are single-threaded event loops
epoll/kqueue: O(1) readiness notification for many connections
sendfile: zero-copy static file delivery
SO_REUSEPORT: kernel-level accept load balancing across workers

sections.title: Nginx: Reverse Proxy, Load Balancing, and TLS
paragraphs: As a reverse proxy, Nginx terminates client connections and opens separate upstream connections to backend servers. proxy_pass, upstream blocks, and keepalive connections to upstreams reduce TCP handshake overhead. Health checks (commercial Plus or open-source modules) remove failed backends from rotation.

Load balancing methods: round-robin (default), least_conn, ip_hash (session stickiness), hash (consistent hashing on URI or custom key). Weighted backends support heterogeneous capacity. For WebSocket and HTTP/2, proxy modules handle protocol upgrade and multiplexing.

TLS termination at Nginx offloads crypto from application servers. ssl_session_cache (shared across workers) and session tickets reduce handshake cost. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (QUIC) modules push protocol handling to the edge. Certificate management (Let's Encrypt, cert-manager sidecars) integrates at this layer.

Rate limiting (limit_req, limit_conn), WAF integration, and request buffering protect backends from abuse and slow clients. Large upload buffering to disk prevents memory exhaustion when clients send slowly — a classic slowloris mitigation combined with timeouts (client_body_timeout, proxy_read_timeout).
bullets: upstream keepalive: reuse backend TCP connections
least_conn vs round-robin: match algorithm to workload skew
TLS session cache/tickets: reduce full handshake frequency
limit_req: token bucket rate limiting per IP or key

sections.title: Kafka and Nginx in System Architecture
paragraphs: A common pattern: Nginx at the edge terminates TLS, serves static assets, load-balances to API servers, and enforces rate limits. API servers publish domain events to Kafka; downstream consumers (search indexer, analytics, email) process independently with at-least-once semantics and idempotent handlers.

Backpressure flows differently in each system. Nginx returns 502/503 when upstreams are saturated — clients see immediate failure or retry. Kafka absorbs write spikes in the log (disk-bound retention) but slow consumers fall behind (consumer lag metric). Monitor lag, rebalance frequency, and under-replicated partitions as Kafka SLOs.

Ordering guarantees: Kafka orders within a partition, not across partitions. Design partition keys so related events co-locate (user_id, order_id). Nginx does not guarantee sticky routing unless ip_hash or consistent hash — session state belongs in Redis or JWT, not local worker memory.

Operational maturity: Kafka needs capacity planning for disk (retention × throughput), partition count, and replication. Nginx needs worker count (usually = CPU cores), connection limits (worker_connections × workers), and upstream timeout tuning aligned with application p99 latency.

Consumer group: cooperative partition assignment with rebalance on membership change
ISR and acks=all: durability vs latency trade-off on produce
At-least-once + idempotent consumer: practical delivery guarantee
Nginx master/worker: single-threaded event loop per worker process
epoll event-driven I/O: scale connections without thread-per-connection
Reverse proxy: TLS termination, load balancing, upstream keepalive
sendfile: zero-copy static file serving

SO_REUSEPORT: kernel distributes accepts across Nginx workers
practices: Size Kafka partitions for target parallelism; key by entity ID for ordering
Use acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 for durable production produces
Implement idempotent consumers with dedup keys or upsert semantics
Monitor consumer lag, under-replicated partitions, and broker disk usage
Set Nginx worker_processes to CPU count; tune worker_connections for peak load
Enable upstream keepalive and align proxy timeouts with application p99
Terminate TLS at Nginx; use limit_req to protect backends from abuse

Consumer rebalance storms from frequent pod restarts — tune session.timeout.ms and use cooperative assignor
Treating Kafka as a task queue with per-message delete — wrong tool; use SQS or dedicated queue
Blocking operations in Nginx Lua or misconfigured upstreams stalling worker event loops
No upstream keepalive — TCP handshake overhead dominates short API calls
Ignoring consumer lag until disk fills or analytics is days behind

examples.title: Event-driven order pipeline
examples.description: Order API (behind Nginx) writes to Postgres and publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka partition keyed by order_id. Inventory, email, and analytics services each consume in separate consumer groups — all receive every event, process at their own pace, and commit offsets after successful handling. Nginx rate-limits checkout endpoints during flash sales.

examples.title: Nginx edge with microservices upstream
examples.description: Nginx terminates TLS, applies WAF rules, and routes /api/users to user-service, /api/orders to order-service via location blocks. Upstream keepalive pools 32 connections per backend. least_conn balances skewed request durations. Static assets served via sendfile with 1-year cache headers — 90% of bytes never hit application servers.

examples.title: Kafka replay for bug fix deployment
examples.description: A bug in the search indexer corrupted documents for 6 hours. Because Kafka retains 7 days of events, the team resets the consumer group offset to the incident start time and replays OrderPlaced events idempotently (upsert by document ID). Without log retention and idempotent writes, manual backfill would take days.

keyTakeaways: Kafka is a replayable commit log — retention and partitions define scale and ordering
Consumer groups enable parallel processing; max consumers = partition count per group
At-least-once with idempotent consumers is the production default for delivery semantics
Nginx scales via event-driven workers — non-blocking I/O and sendfile for efficiency
Edge proxy handles TLS, load balancing, rate limiting — protect and offload backends
Monitor Kafka consumer lag and Nginx upstream 5xx/latency as primary health signals
Partition key design determines ordering scope — choose keys aligned with business invariants
lessons.whyItMatters: Kafka and Nginx form the data plane and control edge of most modern backends. Interview questions about event ordering, consumer lag, and reverse proxy configuration assume you understand internals, not just configuration snippets. Production incidents in both systems trace directly to partition design, rebalance behavior, worker limits, and timeout mismatches.

What happens to in-flight requests when an Nginx worker receives SIGUSR1 reload? What about SIGQUIT shutdown?
Design partition count and consumer group topology for 100K events/sec with 5 downstream processors.
When would you bypass Nginx and expose a service directly behind a cloud load balancer?

lessons.title: Redis & PostgreSQL Internals
lessons.summary: Redis and PostgreSQL sit at opposite ends of the data store spectrum — in-memory structures vs. durable relational pages — yet both appear together in nearly every production stack. Understanding their internal architectures explains why Redis is fast (single-threaded event loop, O(1) structures) and why Postgres queries behave as they do (MVCC, buffer pool, WAL, query planner).

sections.title: Redis: In-Memory Data Structures and Single-Threaded Execution
paragraphs: Redis is primarily an in-memory key-value store with rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams, and more. Each type is implemented with optimized internal encodings — a small hash might use a ziplist (compact contiguous memory) and automatically upgrade to a hash table as it grows.

The core Redis server process is single-threaded for command execution. One event loop (epoll/kqueue) handles thousands of client connections; commands are processed sequentially, eliminating lock contention on data structures. This design is why Redis achieves sub-millisecond latency — no mutex overhead on the hot path.

Persistence is optional and configurable. RDB snapshots fork a child process (copy-on-write) to dump memory to disk periodically. AOF (Append-Only File) logs every write command and replays on restart — fsync policy (always, everysec, no) trades durability for throughput. Most production setups use both: RDB for fast restarts, AOF for minimal data loss.

Eviction policies (allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl, etc.) kick in when maxmemory is reached. Redis is not a cache by default — without maxmemory and eviction, it grows until OOM. Treat explicit TTLs and memory limits as mandatory operational configuration, not optional tuning.
bullets: Single-threaded command execution — no locks on data structures
Encodings upgrade automatically (ziplist → hashtable, intset → set)
RDB: point-in-time snapshot; AOF: command replay log
Streams: log-like structure with consumer groups (Kafka-lite)

sections.title: Redis: Replication, Cluster, and Common Pitfalls
paragraphs: Primary-replica replication is asynchronous by default. Replicas connect to the primary, receive a full sync (RDB transfer) or partial resync (backlog buffer), then stream incremental commands. Read-your-writes is not guaranteed on replicas — a write to primary may not appear on replica for milliseconds, causing stale reads if you route reads to replicas blindly.

Redis Cluster shards data across 16,384 hash slots. Each master owns a slot range; replicas failover via gossip and majority quorum. MOVED and ASK redirects tell clients the correct node. Cluster mode adds operational complexity — multi-key transactions only work within the same hash slot (use hash tags {user:123}.profile and {user:123}.sessions).

Lua scripts and MULTI/EXEC provide atomicity on a single node. There is no cross-slot distributed transaction in cluster mode. For distributed locks, Redlock is controversial — understand clock skew and fencing tokens before trusting Redis locks for financial correctness.

Memory fragmentation, big keys, and hot keys are production killers. A single 100 MB hash key blocks the event loop during deletion. MONITOR and KEYS commands block production — use SCAN instead. Pipeline batches commands to amortize round-trip latency without changing atomicity semantics.
bullets: Async replication → possible stale reads on replicas
Hash slots: 16384 slots partitioned across cluster masters
Hash tags {id} force related keys to same slot for multi-key ops
Pipeline: batch commands; Transaction (MULTI/EXEC): atomic batch on one node

sections.title: PostgreSQL: Pages, Buffer Pool, and MVCC
paragraphs: PostgreSQL stores data in 8 KB pages (blocks) organized in tables and indexes (B-tree default). The shared buffer pool caches hot pages in memory — identical in concept to an OS page cache but managed by Postgres. A sequential scan reads pages from buffer or disk; repeated access benefits from cache warmth.

MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) lets readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Each row has xmin (inserting transaction) and xmax (deleting/updating transaction) system columns. UPDATE creates a new row version; the old version becomes dead tuple until vacuum reclaims space.

Vacuum (autovacuum) is not optional housekeeping — it prevents transaction ID wraparound, reclaims dead tuple space, and updates visibility map bits for index-only scans. Bloat from long-running transactions holding old snapshots is a top Postgres performance incident: a forgotten open transaction blocks vacuum from cleaning millions of dead rows.

Indexes are separate B-tree structures pointing to heap tuples. A query may index scan + heap fetch (random I/O) or bitmap index scan for moderate selectivity. Covering indexes (INCLUDE columns) enable index-only scans when visibility map confirms tuples are visible — a major optimization for read-heavy workloads.
bullets: 8 KB pages in shared_buffers — Postgres-managed cache
MVCC: row versions with xmin/xmax; UPDATE = insert new + mark old dead
VACUUM reclaims dead tuples; autovacuum must keep pace with write rate
B-tree index: default for equality and range; GIN/GiST for full-text, JSON, geo

sections.title: PostgreSQL: WAL, Checkpoints, and the Query Planner
paragraphs: Every change goes to the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) before data pages are flushed to disk. WAL is sequential append — fast on SSD and HDD. On crash recovery, Postgres replays WAL to bring data files to a consistent state. WAL also feeds logical replication and physical streaming replicas.

Checkpoints flush dirty buffer pool pages to data files and create a recovery starting point. Too frequent checkpoints increase I/O; too infrequent checkpoints lengthen crash recovery and increase WAL size. tuning checkpoint_completion_target spreads flush I/O to avoid latency spikes.

The query planner estimates cost using statistics (ANALYZE). It chooses nested loop (small inner), hash join (equi-joins, large tables), or merge join (pre-sorted inputs). Bad plans from stale statistics — a column went from uniform to skewed — cause catastrophic seq scans on billion-row tables. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) is your primary diagnostic tool.

Connection model matters: Postgres uses one process per connection. Thousands of idle connections consume memory and hurt performance — use PgBouncer (transaction or session pooling) in front of the database. Long transactions hold locks and prevent vacuum — set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
bullets: WAL: durability and replication source; sequential writes
Checkpoints: periodic flush of dirty pages to data files
Planner: cost-based; depends on pg_statistic from ANALYZE
PgBouncer: pool connections — essential at high client counts

sections.title: Using Redis and Postgres Together
paragraphs: The canonical pattern: Postgres is the source of truth; Redis is cache, session store, rate limiter, or pub/sub layer. Cache-aside: read Redis first, on miss query Postgres, populate Redis with TTL. Invalidate on write (delete cache key) rather than update-in-place to avoid race conditions.

Write-through and write-behind are alternatives when consistency requirements differ. Sessions and rate limits tolerate loss on Redis failure — rebuild from login or reset counters. Financial balances belong in Postgres with ACID guarantees; never rely on Redis alone for authoritative ledger state.

Hot key mitigation in Redis: local in-process cache (Caffeine) in front of Redis, read replicas for read-heavy keys, or application-level sharding of a hot counter into multiple keys summed at read time. In Postgres: partition large tables, partial indexes for active subsets, and read replicas for analytics (with lag awareness).

Understanding internals lets you tune intentionally: Redis maxmemory-policy and key design; Postgres shared_buffers (~25% RAM), effective_cache_size, work_mem for sorts, and index strategy matched to query patterns. Blind defaults work until scale proves otherwise.

core.title: Redis: In-Memory Data Structures and Single-Threaded Execution
paragraphs: Redis is primarily an in-memory key-value store with rich data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams, and more. Each type is implemented with optimized internal encodings — a small hash might use a ziplist (compact contiguous memory) and automatically upgrade to a hash table as it grows.

The core Redis server process is single-threaded for command execution. One event loop (epoll/kqueue) handles thousands of client connections; commands are processed sequentially, eliminating lock contention on data structures. This design is why Redis achieves sub-millisecond latency — no mutex overhead on the hot path.

Persistence is optional and configurable. RDB snapshots fork a child process (copy-on-write) to dump memory to disk periodically. AOF (Append-Only File) logs every write command and replays on restart — fsync policy (always, everysec, no) trades durability for throughput. Most production setups use both: RDB for fast restarts, AOF for minimal data loss.

Eviction policies (allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl, etc.) kick in when maxmemory is reached. Redis is not a cache by default — without maxmemory and eviction, it grows until OOM. Treat explicit TTLs and memory limits as mandatory operational configuration, not optional tuning.
bullets: Single-threaded command execution — no locks on data structures
Encodings upgrade automatically (ziplist → hashtable, intset → set)
RDB: point-in-time snapshot; AOF: command replay log
Streams: log-like structure with consumer groups (Kafka-lite)

core.title: Redis: Replication, Cluster, and Common Pitfalls
paragraphs: Primary-replica replication is asynchronous by default. Replicas connect to the primary, receive a full sync (RDB transfer) or partial resync (backlog buffer), then stream incremental commands. Read-your-writes is not guaranteed on replicas — a write to primary may not appear on replica for milliseconds, causing stale reads if you route reads to replicas blindly.

Redis Cluster shards data across 16,384 hash slots. Each master owns a slot range; replicas failover via gossip and majority quorum. MOVED and ASK redirects tell clients the correct node. Cluster mode adds operational complexity — multi-key transactions only work within the same hash slot (use hash tags {user:123}.profile and {user:123}.sessions).

Lua scripts and MULTI/EXEC provide atomicity on a single node. There is no cross-slot distributed transaction in cluster mode. For distributed locks, Redlock is controversial — understand clock skew and fencing tokens before trusting Redis locks for financial correctness.

Memory fragmentation, big keys, and hot keys are production killers. A single 100 MB hash key blocks the event loop during deletion. MONITOR and KEYS commands block production — use SCAN instead. Pipeline batches commands to amortize round-trip latency without changing atomicity semantics.
bullets: Async replication → possible stale reads on replicas
Hash slots: 16384 slots partitioned across cluster masters
Hash tags {id} force related keys to same slot for multi-key ops
Pipeline: batch commands; Transaction (MULTI/EXEC): atomic batch on one node

core.title: PostgreSQL: Pages, Buffer Pool, and MVCC
paragraphs: PostgreSQL stores data in 8 KB pages (blocks) organized in tables and indexes (B-tree default). The shared buffer pool caches hot pages in memory — identical in concept to an OS page cache but managed by Postgres. A sequential scan reads pages from buffer or disk; repeated access benefits from cache warmth.

MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) lets readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Each row has xmin (inserting transaction) and xmax (deleting/updating transaction) system columns. UPDATE creates a new row version; the old version becomes dead tuple until vacuum reclaims space.

Vacuum (autovacuum) is not optional housekeeping — it prevents transaction ID wraparound, reclaims dead tuple space, and updates visibility map bits for index-only scans. Bloat from long-running transactions holding old snapshots is a top Postgres performance incident: a forgotten open transaction blocks vacuum from cleaning millions of dead rows.

Indexes are separate B-tree structures pointing to heap tuples. A query may index scan + heap fetch (random I/O) or bitmap index scan for moderate selectivity. Covering indexes (INCLUDE columns) enable index-only scans when visibility map confirms tuples are visible — a major optimization for read-heavy workloads.
bullets: 8 KB pages in shared_buffers — Postgres-managed cache
MVCC: row versions with xmin/xmax; UPDATE = insert new + mark old dead
VACUUM reclaims dead tuples; autovacuum must keep pace with write rate
B-tree index: default for equality and range; GIN/GiST for full-text, JSON, geo

core.title: PostgreSQL: WAL, Checkpoints, and the Query Planner
paragraphs: Every change goes to the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) before data pages are flushed to disk. WAL is sequential append — fast on SSD and HDD. On crash recovery, Postgres replays WAL to bring data files to a consistent state. WAL also feeds logical replication and physical streaming replicas.

Checkpoints flush dirty buffer pool pages to data files and create a recovery starting point. Too frequent checkpoints increase I/O; too infrequent checkpoints lengthen crash recovery and increase WAL size. tuning checkpoint_completion_target spreads flush I/O to avoid latency spikes.

The query planner estimates cost using statistics (ANALYZE). It chooses nested loop (small inner), hash join (equi-joins, large tables), or merge join (pre-sorted inputs). Bad plans from stale statistics — a column went from uniform to skewed — cause catastrophic seq scans on billion-row tables. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) is your primary diagnostic tool.

Connection model matters: Postgres uses one process per connection. Thousands of idle connections consume memory and hurt performance — use PgBouncer (transaction or session pooling) in front of the database. Long transactions hold locks and prevent vacuum — set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
bullets: WAL: durability and replication source; sequential writes
Checkpoints: periodic flush of dirty pages to data files
Planner: cost-based; depends on pg_statistic from ANALYZE
PgBouncer: pool connections — essential at high client counts
